--- Special K Presentation Workbench is a modder's playground for reshaping how Special K presents itself, from on-screen overlays to the little touches that make a session feel yours. Think of it as a set of dials and levers for the presentation layer, built for tinkerers who'd rather tweak than settle. Everything here stays close to Special K's own presentation flow, so your changes slot in naturally instead of fighting the host. alternative it open, poke around, and make the presentation side of Special K behave the way you always wanted. ## 📋 System Requirements - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features **Live Framing & Composition Control** — Nudge the camera, crop the frame, and dial in the presentation angle without ever leaving the scene. The Workbench hands you direct control over how every moment reads on screen. **Real-Time Parameter Tweaking** — Slide, scrub, and swing values on the fly while everything renders live. No restart loops, no guesswork — just immediate feedback as you sculpt the look. **Preset Vault & Snapshots** — Save your favorite setups as reusable presets, then swap between them at a moment's notice. A safe snapshot system means you can experiment boldly and roll back without fear. **Layered Scene Staging** — Stack, blend, and sequence presentation elements on independent layers. Want a subtle overlay here and a bold cut there? Build it your way, layer by layer. **Modder-Friendly Tuning Hooks** — Everything that matters is exposed and hackable. Twist the knobs, remap the bindings, and wire the Workbench into your own workflows — it's built to bend, not break. **Lightweight Runtime Footprint** — Runs lean so your presentation stays smooth and snappy, whether you're previewing a quick shot or orchestrating a full showcase. **Iteration Without Friction** — Built around the way modders actually work: fast edits, instant previews, and zero ceremony between ideas and results. ## How It Works Special K Presentation Workbench doesn't fight your game — it sits between the frame buffer and the display, quietly rewriting the rules of presentation on the fly. At its core is a lightweight hook layer that observes the swap chain each frame and swaps in its own scheduling logic, so you keep full control over pacing without touching the engine's own render path. Every frame is captured at the presentation boundary and passed through a stack of composable stages: pacing, frame synthesis, and latency shaping. Each stage is independent, ordered, and hot-swappable from the workbench overlay, meaning you can tune behavior mid-session while watching the results in real time. If a stage misbehaves, the pipeline falls back to the vanilla present call — your game never learns it was interrupted. The magic lives in the **Workbench**, an in-game panel that lays the pipeline bare. Tweak pacing curves, dial in frame generation ratios, or profile per-frame timings without a single restart. Settings persist on disk and load automatically, so your carefully tuned setup greets you the next time you launch. Modders can define custom stages in simple config files and drop them straight into the stage list — no recompilation, no patching the binary. Compatibility is handled defensively: the workbench detects the presentation model in use, adapts its hooks to match, and quietly steps aside when it encounters something it doesn't understand. When it steps back, the game presents exactly as it did before, byte for byte. That means you can leave it installed everywhere and only engage it where it belongs. Under the hood it's all about timing. The scheduler maintains a rolling model of present intervals and uses it to predict the next frame — then decides, frame by frame, whether to hold, release, or synthesize. This is what lets the workbench smooth out stutter spikes and push presentation cadence beyond the engine's native limits without tearing or sync artifacts. The result feels less like a mod and more like a re-tuned pipeline running underneath everything else. ## Modules and Settings ### Scene Assembly Module The Scene Assembly module provides the core workspace for building and arranging the elements that make up a presentation. - Scene element placement lets you add staging, framing and layering components to the current scene, with each addition immediately reflected in the presentation view. - Element reordering controls allow you to move items forward or backward in the layering order, adjusting how components overlap and read against one another. - Separate scene units keep different setups isolated, so editing one arrangement does not disturb another. ### Sequence Timing Module The Sequence Timing module defines the order and pacing of presentation steps so a scene plays out as a deliberate sequence. - Step ordering controls let you arrange when each presentation state occurs relative to the others. - Pacing adjustments shift individual steps earlier or later, changing the rhythm between them. - Transition smoothing settings determine whether changes between states blend gradually or switch abruptly. ### Camera and Framing Module The Camera and Framing module governs the viewpoint used during a presentation so framing stays consistent across a scene. - Angle and distance controls reposition the viewpoint relative to the subject being presented. - Focus target selection determines which element the framing centers on. - Per-scene framing values keep each scene's viewpoint independent from the others. ### Visual Parameter Module The Visual Parameter module tunes how displayed presentation elements look within a given scene. - Independent controls for intensity, contrast and emphasis let you adjust each visual property on its own. - In-context previewing shows parameter changes against the scene as they are tuned. - Scene-bound values keep adjustments attached to the scene they belong to rather than spreading across the whole workspace. ### Preset Library Module The Preset Library module stores configured setups so they can be reused without rebuilding them. - Save, rename and duplicate actions let you maintain multiple presentation styles side by side. - Applying a preset restores its arrangement, timing and visual settings to the active scene. - Removal controls clear presets that are no longer needed. ### Preview and Comparison Module The Preview and Comparison module supports inspecting and refining scenes before they are used in play. - Preview mode displays the active scene as it will read once committed. - Variant switching lets you move between saved versions and observe differences in arrangement, timing and framing. - Discard actions make it easy to drop a change that does not read well and return to the prior state. ### Additional Settings - Workspace grouping and labeling options organize scenes and presets into recognizable groups for easier navigation. - Last-selection retention reopens the workbench on the item you were last working with. - Configuration persistence keeps user adjustments between sessions so tuning work is not lost. - Revert controls restore individual scenes, presets or parameters to their previous configuration, keeping experimentation reversible. ## Usage Scenarios ### Composing a Multi-Layered Stage Scene **Goal:** Build a presentation scene with staging, framing and layered elements arranged in a deliberate order so the composition reads clearly. **Steps:** 1. Open the Scene Assembly module and create a new, separate scene unit so the arrangement stays isolated from existing setups. 2. Place staging, framing and layering components into the scene, watching each addition appear in the presentation view. 3. Use the element reordering controls to move components forward or backward until the overlap between layers reads the way you want. 4. Switch to the Camera and Framing module and set the angle, distance and focus target for this scene only. 5. Review the composed arrangement in the Preview and Comparison module before leaving it as the committed version. **Expected result:** A self-contained scene where the layers stack in the intended order and the viewpoint frames the subject consistently, with the framing values stored against that scene rather than shared with others. ### Tuning Sequence Pacing and Transitions **Goal:** Define the order of presentation steps and adjust the rhythm so transitions feel deliberate instead of default. **Steps:** 1. In the Sequence Timing module, arrange the presentation steps so each state occurs in the desired order. 2. Shift individual steps earlier or later to adjust the pacing between them. 3. Set transition smoothing so changes between states either blend gradually or switch abruptly, depending on the feel you want. 4. Open Preview mode and step through the sequence to check how the timing reads. 5. If a change does not work, use the discard action to return to the prior state and try a different pacing. **Expected result:** A controllable sequence the user can review step by step, with pacing and transition smoothing that match the intended feel and can be reverted if an adjustment does not read well. ### Maintaining Multiple Presets and Styles **Goal:** Keep several distinct presentation styles available and reuse them across scenes without rebuilding each one. **Steps:** 1. Configure a scene's arrangement, timing and visual parameters using the Scene Assembly, Sequence Timing and Visual Parameter modules. 2. Save the configured setup as a preset in the Preset Library, then rename or duplicate it to create a variation. 3. Repeat for additional styles so several presets sit side by side in the library. 4. Apply a preset to the active scene to restore its arrangement, timing and visual settings. 5. Group and label the scenes and presets in the workspace so each style is easy to find, and keep the last active selection for continuity. **Expected result:** A workspace holding multiple named presets that can be applied to scenes on demand, with visual parameters such as intensity, contrast and emphasis staying bound to the scene they belong to, and adjustments retained between sessions. ## Installation Getting the Workbench humming is less about wrangling files and more about inviting a new instrument into your presentation rig. Here's the ritual, from first breath to first frame. **1. Choose your den.** Pick a home for the Workbench where it will live alongside your other projects — a dedicated folder with a name you'll recognize at a glance. A tidy den makes for a happy tinkerer, and future-you will thank present-you for the foresight. **2. Gather the workshop pieces.** The Workbench arrives as a self-contained bundle. Unpack it into the den you carved out and take a slow tour of what's inside: the core presentation engine, the preset scaffolding, and the starter assets that give you something to push live the very first time you fire it up. Touch nothing yet — just look. Know your tools before you turn them on. **3. Wire it into your presentation pipeline.** Point your host presentation environment at the Workbench's core entry point, following the layout described in the bundle. If your host supports custom module directories, drop the Workbench in and let it be discovered naturally; otherwise register it by name in your host's configuration and confirm it answers the roll call. **4. Flip the master switch.** Launch the Workbench for the first time and check that its dashboard responds: presets should populate, starter assets should resolve, and the status readout should greet you without complaint. If something feels off, resist the urge to flail — retrace your steps from the den to the entry point; nine times in ten, a missed path is the culprit. **5. Take your first swing.** Load a starter preset and drive it end to end. Get a feel for how the Workbench moves — how transitions linger, how timing breathes, where the seams show. You're not looking for perfection; you're learning the instrument's voice. **6. Personalize the workshop.** Once you're confident, begin carving your own presets and dropping your own assets into the den. Rename the starter scaffolding to something that belongs to *you*, and keep the originals safe in a corner. Great mods are built on the wreckage of many brave first attempts. **A few hard-won notes from the bench:** back up your den before any major reshuffle; keep the Workbench in its own folder so upgrades never scramble your custom work; and when in doubt, strip back to the starter bundle and rebuild. The Workbench is forgiving — it wants to be played. Treat it like a collaborator, not a tool. Now go make something worth presenting. ## Compatibility The Workbench speaks fluent Special K, so it plays nicest with setups already running Special K's presentation layer. If you've got Special K installed and humming, you're already home. Bring your favorite HDR, latency, and frame-pacing tweaks into the Workbench and let it riff on top of them — this mod was built to jam with Special K, not fight it for the spotlight. Version-wise, treat the Workbench as a picky collaborator: it expects a reasonably current Special K build that exposes the presentation hooks it leans on. Older builds may shrug it off, or worse, cause a cold shoulder at launch. When in doubt, update Special K first, then see if the Workbench perks up. Because the Workbench pokes at the presentation pipeline, anything else that also wants a hand on the same knobs — overlays, injectors, frame-limiting helpers, capture tools, or other presentation-layer mods — is a potential turf war. Duplicates vying for the same controls can cause flicker, stalls, or settings that quietly refuse to stick. Best practice: run one presentation handler at a time, or at least know who's holding the wheel. A few practical notes from the workshop floor: - **Single-host discipline:** If another tool is already injecting overlays or steering the presentation path, either retire it or disable its overlapping features before firing up the Workbench. - **Graphics driver quirks:** Unusual driver-side scaling, exotic HDR modes, or multi-GPU setups can nudge the Workbench into odd behavior. If something looks off, fall back to a plainer configuration and add complexity back one piece at a time. - **Game-agnostic, but not game-blind:** The Workbench doesn't tailor itself to individual titles. Some games tolerate its meddling gracefully; others want specific launch flags or in-game settings to keep the peace. Experimentation is part of the craft. - **Storefront and launcher neutrality:** Storefront wrappers and launchers generally stay out of the way, but aggressive anti-tamper or sandboxing layers may block injection entirely. That's a boundary the Workbench can't tunnel through. - **Fresh-copy rule of thumb:** When troubleshooting, start from a clean Special K profile and a vanilla game config, confirm the Workbench is lively, then reintroduce your other tooling one item at a time. Blame whoever breaks first — it's usually the newcomer. If you hit a clash, the fastest path to clarity is to isolate: disable everything else, confirm the Workbench behaves, and then reintroduce your other tooling one item at a time. Compatibility isn't a promise here — it's a conversation, and the Workbench is a good listener when you give it room to breathe. ## Credits No work of wizardry happens in a vacuum, and the Special K Presentation Workbench is no exception. This tool exists because a whole chorus of tinkerers, tuners, and late-night frame-chasers believed presentations deserved better than a stutter. First and loudest, thanks to everyone who ever wrestled a stubborn shader or chased a frame-time spike into the small hours and then shared what they learned instead of hoarding it. You know who you are, and so do your crash logs. To the early adopters who ran the Workbench before it was safe to run and reported back with precise, reproducible, gloriously nerdy bug reports: you are the reason the rough edges got sanded smooth. Every sanity-checked preset and every "it just works now" moment carries your fingerprints. To the modders who built on top of these ideas, forked their own experiments, or quietly patched something and sent it upstream: this project is a conversation, and you kept it going. And finally, to the patient souls who tested across weird hardware nobody else had, who confirmed that one elusive fix actually fixed it, and who kept the encouragement coming when the build refused to compile — you turned a pile of good intentions into something playable. Special K Presentation Workbench is dedicated to the idea that polish is a community sport. Thank you for playing. ## License The Special K Presentation Workbench is released under a permissive open-mod license. Tinker with it, remix it, fold it into your own presentation pipelines, or ship it inside a content pack — you're free to build on this work as long as you keep the original credits intact and don't misrepresent the workbench as your own creation. Bundled assets, sample presets, and any third-party knick-knacks carry their own terms, so give those a read before redistributing them. If you improve the workbench, sharing your changes back is warmly encouraged but never required; the modding scene thrives on give-and-take. Above all, use it in good faith — respect the effort poured into this bench, credit the hands that built it, and pass the craft forward.

--- http2shell-brotli-impact-review is a standalone analysis utility for evaluating how Brotli-compressed HTTP/2 payloads affect shell-based tooling and downstream processing in the http2shell workflow. It parses captured streams, measures compression ratios and decompression costs, and reports concrete impact metrics for each tested input. All checks run locally against supplied artifacts, with deterministic outputs and no external dependencies at runtime. Results are intended to support risk assessment and remediation decisions with reproducible, verifiable data. ## 📋 System Requirements - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features - Parses HTTP/2 frame streams and isolates HEADERS and DATA frames for per-stream analysis, preserving HPACK-compressed header blocks for inspection without requiring prior decompression. - Decompresses Brotli-encoded response bodies and extracts compression metadata (window size, block count, ratio) to support impact assessment of Brotli handling on shell-oriented payloads. - Computes per-stream compression ratios and size deltas between compressed and decompressed payloads, with configurable thresholds for flagging anomalous expansion or contraction. - Detects and reports HPACK dynamic table behavior, including header field indexing patterns and table size updates, to surface state-dependent header compression effects. - Emits structured findings in JSON with stable schema fields (stream ID, frame type, byte counts, ratio, classification) for downstream tooling and reproducible review. - Operates deterministically on captured inputs: identical input yields identical output, with no network calls or telemetry during analysis. - Validates Brotli stream integrity and reports truncation, malformed blocks, or trailing data separately from decompression results. - Supports batch processing of multiple capture files with per-file summaries and aggregate statistics. - Includes a rule-based classifier that maps observed Brotli and HPACK characteristics to documented impact categories, with rule identifiers included in output for auditability. - Runs as a local, dependency-minimal process with no elevated privileges required and no persistent state written outside the designated output directory. ## How it works The tool operates as a static review harness rather than an active exploitation framework. It ingests a user-supplied corpus of HTTP/2 traffic captures and configuration snapshots, then evaluates each sample against a fixed rule set describing how Brotli-compressed response bodies interact with shell-oriented payload delivery paths. Processing proceeds in four deterministic stages. First, input normalization parses the capture or configuration into a canonical record: stream identifiers, header blocks, compression flags, content-encoding declarations, and body digests. Second, a compression classifier inspects the declared and observed encoding of each response body, distinguishing Brotli from identity, gzip, and deflate, and flagging mismatches between advertised and actual encodings. Third, a rule engine applies the review checks, comparing decompressed body characteristics against known impact indicators such as size asymmetry between compressed and expanded payloads, abrupt stream resets during body transmission, and header ordering that affects intermediary buffering. Fourth, results are aggregated into a per-sample verdict with supporting evidence references to the originating record fields. All analysis is performed locally against the provided samples. No network egress is initiated by the review process, and no sample content is transmitted off-host. The rule set is versioned and bundled with the tool so that verdicts are reproducible across runs; each report records the rule-set version and input digests, allowing independent re-verification. Output is emitted in machine-readable form and includes, for every finding, the rule identifier, the affected stream, and the exact field offsets consulted, so conclusions can be audited without re-running the tool. ## Modules and Settings ### Review Scenario Configuration Establishes the saved baseline that every other module draws from, so that comparisons and reports remain consistent across repeated review runs. - Target traffic pattern selector defines the request sequence shape and session characteristics the rest of the review will reference. - Inspection environment profile records the monitoring and filtering context in which the modeled traffic is observed. - Scenario persistence saves the profile for reuse, letting later runs and handoffs start from identical conditions. ### HTTP/2 Shell Traffic Modeling Produces a structured trace of shell-oriented HTTP/2 exchanges so reviewers can examine how request framing and stream behavior are represented. - Stream grouping control adjusts how requests are distributed across streams, changing the shape of the recorded trace. - Session lifetime expression sets how long the modeled session persists within the scenario. - Trace view presents the modeled exchanges in a comparable format for cross-scenario analysis. ### Brotli Payload Impact Comparison Runs Brotli-encoded and equivalent uncompressed payloads within the same scenario to isolate the effect of the encoding choice. - Encoding declaration settings control how encoded bodies are identified to the inspection layer. - Body segmentation option adjusts how encoded payloads are divided across the exchange. - Side-by-side comparison view shows how each variant is described by inspection, supporting attribution of observed effects to encoding. ### Inspection and Detection Outcome Reporting Collects per-exchange treatment into the review's core deliverable, recording how the configured inspection setup handled each modeled exchange. - Outcome emphasis selector lets the user prioritize content visibility, classification, or policy action in the report. - Annotation support attaches reviewer notes to specific exchanges and scenarios. - Report listing pairs each scenario and variant with its observed outcome for structured review. ### Policy Rule Evaluation Checks whether attached policy rules produce the expected decisions for modeled HTTP/2 shell traffic and Brotli-encoded payloads. - Rule attachment links policy conditions to a scenario so decisions are evaluated within that context. - Between-run rule adjustment reveals which conditions change outcomes across iterations. - Per-exchange decision record shows rule matches and the resulting actions for each modeled exchange. ### Controlled Variation and Replay Replays scenarios with single deliberate changes so reviewers can identify which factor drives an observed outcome. - Parameter-level adjustment changes one setting at a time while holding the rest of the scenario fixed. - Paired-run output highlights differences between runs, such as toggling Brotli encoding on or off. - Variation history keeps changed parameters visible alongside results for traceability. ### Additional Settings Optional controls that support review workflow and handoff without altering the core scenario logic. - Evidence selection chooses which scenario profiles, run records, and annotations are included in a review bundle. - Bundle packaging produces a self-contained handoff artifact another analyst can open under the same conditions. - Run labeling tags scenarios and replays for easier identification during later comparison. - Comparison baseline designation marks one run as the reference point for variation and outcome diffs. ## Usage Scenarios ### Reviewing Brotli Encoding Effect on Inspection Visibility **Goal:** A security engineer wants to understand whether enabling Brotli payload encoding changes how much of a shell-oriented HTTP/2 exchange remains visible to the inspection layer, before deciding whether encoding deserves extra scrutiny in the review. **Steps:** 1. Create a review scenario profile in Review Scenario Configuration, selecting the target traffic pattern for the shell-oriented request sequence and recording the inspection environment profile. 2. Model the exchange in HTTP/2 Shell Traffic Modeling, adjusting stream grouping and session lifetime expression so the trace reflects the intended session shape. 3. Run the same scenario twice in Brotli Payload Impact Comparison: once with Brotli encoding enabled and once with an equivalent uncompressed payload, using encoding declaration settings and body segmentation to define each variant. 4. Use the side-by-side comparison view to inspect how each variant is described by the inspection layer. 5. Emphasize content visibility in Inspection and Detection Outcome Reporting and annotate the exchanges where the two variants diverge. **Expected result:** A report listing both variants with their observed outcomes, showing which exchanges differed in content visibility between the Brotli-encoded and uncompressed runs, with reviewer annotations marking the exchanges where the encoding choice appeared to affect inspection. ### Evaluating Policy Rules Against Modeled HTTP/2 Shell Traffic **Goal:** A defensive analyst wants to check whether the organization's attached policy rules produce the expected decisions when shell-oriented HTTP/2 traffic carries Brotli-encoded payloads. **Steps:** 1. Load an existing scenario profile from Review Scenario Configuration so the policy evaluation runs under the same conditions as prior reviews. 2. Attach the relevant policy conditions to the scenario using Rule Attachment in Policy Rule Evaluation. 3. Run the scenario with Brotli encoding enabled and examine the per-exchange decision record for rule matches and resulting actions. 4. Adjust one rule condition between runs to see whether the decision changes, keeping the rest of the scenario fixed. 5. Tag each run with a label for later identification and select policy action as the emphasis in Inspection and Detection Outcome Reporting. **Expected result:** A per-exchange decision record for each run showing which rules matched and what action followed, plus a report section highlighting policy actions, making it clear which rule conditions changed the outcome when Brotli-encoded payloads were present. ### Isolating a Single Factor Through Controlled Replay and Packaging a Handoff **Goal:** A red-team reviewer wants to determine whether a specific setting — Brotli encoding being switched on or off — is responsible for an observed difference, and then hand the findings to another analyst for reproduction. **Steps:** 1. Designate the initial run as the comparison baseline in Additional Settings so subsequent replays are measured against it. 2. Use Controlled Variation and Replay to adjust only the Brotli encoding toggle at the parameter level, holding the remaining scenario settings fixed. 3. Review the paired-run output and variation history to confirm the changed parameter and the resulting differences. 4. Add annotations to the exchanges of interest and tag each replay run for identification. 5. Select the baseline scenario profile, both run records, and the annotations for evidence selection, then package the review bundle. **Expected result:** A set of paired runs whose differences are attributable to the single toggled setting, accompanied by a variation history listing the changed parameter, and a self-contained review bundle that another analyst can open to inspect the same scenarios, run records, and annotations. ## Privacy This tool operates entirely offline and does not transmit, collect, or store any data beyond the local filesystem on which it is executed. No telemetry, analytics, crash reporting, or usage statistics are generated or sent anywhere. The tool makes no outbound network connections during normal operation; any network activity observed must originate from the user's own environment or from explicitly invoked components outside this project's scope. --- Arc Raiders Norvena delivers focused gameplay assistance and clean information overlays that keep you locked into every raid. Get real-time intel where it matters—loot cues, threat awareness, and objective context surfaced without clutter. The overlay stays readable under pressure and respects the core Arc Raiders experience, enhancing awareness instead of rewriting the game. Built for players who want an edge without unnecessary overhauls. ## ✅ Requirements - Windows 10 or Windows 11 - PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) - Active network connection - No admin rights needed ## Features - **Combat-awareness overlays** — see threat indicators, player positions, and engagement cues rendered directly over your screen so you can read a fight before it reads you. - **Loot and extraction intel** — surface nearby loot spawns, extraction points, and high-value containers without breaking your flow through the map. - **Live HUD that stays out of the way** — minimal, configurable overlays that feed you the numbers that matter and stay quiet when they don't. - **Real-time situational feeds** — proximity alerts, event timers, and status readouts piped in as they happen, so you're never caught flat-footed. - **Player and entity tracking** — keep tabs on movement around you with clear, readable markers that update live. - **Map-level information layer** — layered intel on objectives, routes, and points of interest you can toggle on demand. ## How it works Arc Raiders Norvena runs alongside the game and reads what the client already exposes — session state, entity data, and UI values — then turns that raw feed into clean, readable assistance. Nothing is injected into the game loop and no game files are touched, so the experience stays the same while the information gets sharper. At its core is a lightweight overlay layer. It hooks the data it needs, normalizes it, and renders it on top of your screen in real time. Updates land frame-synced, so what you see matches what's actually happening in the raid — no stale numbers, no lag between the world and the readout. Gameplay assistance is the priority. Information overlays surface the details that matter mid-run: positioning context, entity awareness, and status readouts delivered in a compact HUD that stays out of your sightline until you need it. Everything is tuned for fast parsing — glance, absorb, move on. The overlay is fully configurable. Toggle individual panels, reposition the HUD, adjust opacity and scale, and dial visibility per element so the screen shows exactly what you want and nothing more. Profiles let you swap layouts between sessions without redoing setup. Under the hood, Norvena keeps a clean separation between data capture, processing, and rendering. That means low overhead, predictable performance, and a stable footprint even during heavy encounters. It assists and informs — it doesn't rewrite the game. ## Modules and Settings ### Target Awareness Overlay Surfaces nearby entities so you can read a room before stepping into it. The overlay feeds the same awareness that the aim and route modules rely on, so what you see here shapes how the rest of arc-raiders-norvena behaves during a raid. - Entity type filters let you choose whether opponents, creatures, or points of interest are shown. - Range control sets how far out markers are drawn, so the overlay stays useful without covering the whole screen. - Marker style options adjust size and clarity of the drawn indicators to match your display and preferences. - Toggle the overlay independently of other modules to keep awareness on while combat aids stay off. ### Loot and Container Highlighting Makes containers, dropped items, and extraction-relevant objects stand out so you can plan a route instead of sweeping blindly. It works alongside route guidance by marking the objects worth detouring for. - Category and tier filters decide which item groups are emphasized, keeping low-value clutter from pulling your attention. - Highlight style controls let you tune color and intensity so markers remain readable against different environments. - Range limiting confines highlighting to nearby objects, which keeps the screen calm during fast movement. - Works as a standalone aid or paired with the overlay to combine entity and loot awareness in one view. ### Aim Assistance Configuration Provides adjustable aim assistance you can shape to different weapons and engagement distances, rather than a single fixed behavior. It reads weapon context from the profiles you set up in the presets module. - Assist strength control determines how much correction is applied when tracking a target. - Activation area sizing sets how close your aim must be before assistance engages. - Fire mode selection lets you apply assistance to hip-fire, aimed fire, or both depending on your habits. - Per-weapon tuning keeps the assist appropriate for close-quarters and long-range engagements alike. ### Recoil and Spread Compensation Compensates weapon recoil and spread so sustained fire stays closer to your intended point of aim. It complements aim assistance by handling the firing pattern while the assist handles tracking. - Per-weapon profiles let each weapon carry its own compensation behavior. - Response aggressiveness adjusts how strongly compensation follows each shot, from subtle to pronounced. - Spread handling can be enabled separately from recoil so you tune only the behavior you need. - Disabling compensation for selected weapons keeps familiar guns feeling unchanged. ### Movement and Traversal Aids Smooths common movement actions so fast traversal produces fewer fumbled inputs. These aids operate independently of combat modules and stay active whether or not you are engaged. - Individual toggles for sprinting, vaulting, and tight-terrain navigation let you enable only the aids you want. - Sensitivity adjustment tunes how responsive each traversal aid feels. - A combined mode coordinates multiple aids so they do not fight each other during complex movement. - Aids can be switched off per raid without altering your saved presets. ### Extraction and Route Guidance Surfaces extraction points and suggests a heading based on your current position, giving you direction when a raid turns unfavorable. It consumes awareness data from the overlay so guidance reflects what is actually around you. - Extraction type prioritization decides which exit options are emphasized in the guidance. - Detail level control adjusts how much route information is displayed versus a simple heading. - Guidance refreshes as you move, keeping suggestions aligned with your position. - Route guidance and loot highlighting can be combined to balance looting with a timely exit. ### Additional Settings - Preset save and load lets you switch between named configurations for different loadouts without rebuilding them. - Shared option selection controls which settings carry across presets, keeping consistent behavior between profiles. - Session status readout summarizes active modules and the current profile so you can confirm your setup before a raid. - Recent adjustment review shows what changed during the session, helping you catch an option left on or off unintentionally. ## Usage Scenarios ### Cautious Approach to a Hot Compound **Goal:** Scout a contested compound before committing, so the user knows whether to push, wait, or reroute. **Steps:** 1. Open the Target Awareness Overlay and enable only opponents and points of interest, leaving creature markers off for a cleaner view. 2. Set the range control to a mid-distance so markers appear before the user is inside the compound, and adjust marker size for readability on their display. 3. Review the entity filters mid-approach to confirm no unexpected marker types are crowding the screen. 4. Keep aim and recoil modules disabled for this raid, since the plan is reconnaissance and an early exit rather than a fight. **Expected result:** A real-time view of nearby opponents and points of interest drawn at the chosen range, letting the user decide to hold position or take another path without switching any combat aids on. ### Loot-Focused Run With a Timed Exit **Goal:** Sweep a location efficiently for valuable items while still reaching extraction before the raid becomes dangerous. **Steps:** 1. Enable Loot and Container Highlighting and use category and tier filters to emphasize only the item groups worth detouring for. 2. Apply range limiting so highlights stay confined to nearby objects and the screen remains calm during fast movement. 3. Turn on Extraction and Route Guidance with the preferred extraction types prioritized and detail level set to a full route suggestion. 4. Combine the route guidance with loot highlighting so detours stay roughly on the way to the chosen exit. 5. Before starting the raid, check the session status readout to confirm the active modules match this plan. **Expected result:** Containers and dropped items that match the filters stand out as the user moves, while the guidance shows a heading toward a prioritized extraction that updates as the player's position changes. ### Close-Quarters Loadout Tuning **Goal:** Configure combat aids that suit a close-quarters loadout without changing how the user's familiar long-range weapon behaves. **Steps:** 1. Open Aim Assistance Configuration, set assist strength to a moderate level, shrink the activation area, and select hip-fire as the fire mode for the close-quarters weapon. 2. In Recoil and Spread Compensation, create a per-weapon profile for that weapon and raise response aggressiveness, leaving spread handling enabled. 3. Select the long-range weapon and disable compensation for it so it keeps its familiar feel. 4. Adjust the activation area and per-weapon aim tuning so the assist behaves differently at close and long distances. 5. Save the whole setup as a named preset, and use shared option selection to decide which settings should carry over from the user's other profiles. **Expected result:** The close-quarters weapon benefits from steadier tracking and a more predictable firing pattern, the long-range weapon behaves as before, and the named preset can be loaded again next session without rebuilding each option. ## Configuration Tune Norvena to match how you play. Every assist and overlay is controlled from a single config file—flip modules on or off, set hotkeys, adjust overlay placement, and dial in exactly how much information hits your screen without touching anything you don't want changed. **Core toggles** - Master switch for all gameplay assistance and information overlays—kill it and Norvena goes fully passive. - Per-module enable flags so you can run only the overlays you care about. - Safe-mode preset that disables everything except read-only info displays. **Gameplay assistance** - Aim assist strength, smoothing, and activation radius—separate values for hip-fire and ADS. - Recoil compensation curve with per-weapon-class multipliers. - Target priority rules: nearest, lowest health, or threat-weighted. - Trigger conditions and cooldowns so assists only kick in when you want them. **Information overlays** - Toggle individual overlays: player status, threat indicators, loot and objective markers, timers, and resource readouts. - Position, scale, opacity, and anchor point per overlay element. - Color and icon themes with a high-contrast option for readability. - Density presets—minimal, standard, or full—so the HUD stays clean at a glance. **Hotkeys and input** - Rebind every toggle to a key or mouse button. - Hold-to-activate vs. toggle behavior per module. - Conflict detection so binds don't collide with in-game controls. **Profiles and presets** - Save and load named profiles for different playstyles or sessions. - Import and export profiles locally to share your setup. - Per-profile hotkey maps and overlay layouts. **Performance and safety** - Frame-rate cap for overlay rendering and an update-interval setting to keep overhead low. - Logging verbosity and a debug overlay for tuning. - Validation on load that flags bad values and falls back to sane defaults instead of breaking. Defaults are balanced for immediate use—drop in, enable what you need, and adjust from there. Changes apply on reload or via the in-app config hotkey. ## FAQ **Is this a full game overhaul?** No. Arc Raiders Norvena is strictly a gameplay assistance and information layer. It doesn't replace core mechanics, rewrite balance, or inject new content. If you're expecting a total conversion, this isn't it — and that's by design. **What does the assistance actually do?** It surfaces what the game already knows but doesn't always show you cleanly: situational awareness cues, contextual prompts, and real-time feedback that help you read the fight and react faster. Think of it as a smarter HUD, not a different game. **Do the information overlays change how the game plays?** They change what you *see*, not what the game *does*. Overlays feed you data — positioning, state, timing — so your decisions get sharper. The underlying simulation runs exactly as it always has. **Will this get me flagged or break my setup?** Norvena operates as an external assistance and information layer. It doesn't patch game files or alter memory in ways that rewrite gameplay logic. That said, always check the terms of service for the platform you're playing on — that's on you, not the tool. **Is it heavy? Will it tank my frames?** No. The overlay and assistance systems are lightweight by design. If you can run the base game comfortably, Norvena rides along without meaningful overhead. **Can I tune what gets shown?** Yes. Configuration controls which overlays and assistance elements are active, so you can run a minimal cue set or a fuller information panel depending on your preference and screen real estate. **Does it work out of the box?** It ships with sensible defaults so you can jump in immediately. Tune it later once you know what you actually want on screen — most players do. **What it is not:** Not a gameplay enhancement suite, not a content mod, not a rebalance patch. It's information and assistance for players who want to play better with the game they already have. ## Disclaimer Arc Raiders Norvena is a gameplay assistance tool built for Arc Raiders. It provides information overlays and gameplay assistance features intended to enhance your situational awareness and decision-making during raids. It does not modify game files, inject into the game process, or alter core game logic. All information surfaced by Norvena is derived from publicly visible game data and your own inputs. Use it at your own discretion. Norvena is an unofficial third-party project and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the developers or publishers of Arc Raiders. Game updates, anti-gameplay enhancement changes, or terms of service revisions may affect functionality or viability at any time. You are responsible for understanding and complying with the rules that apply to your account and platform. Norvena is provided as-is, without warranty of any kind, and the maintainers accept no liability for account actions, data loss, or other consequences arising from its use.

--- `opencode-project-workbench` is a command-line tool for managing the lifecycle of OpenCode project workspaces, covering creation, configuration, and cleanup through a single executable interface. It targets developers who maintain multiple projects and need repeatable, scriptable operations instead of manual directory handling. The tool operates strictly on local project state and does not attempt to manage dependencies, version control, or remote resources. Its scope is limited to the operations documented in its command reference; anything outside that scope is intentionally left to other tooling. Behavior is deterministic given the same inputs, and all commands fail loudly rather than guessing at intent. ## 🔧 Requirements - Windows 10 or Windows 11 - PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) - Active network connection - No admin rights needed ## Features - **Project-scoped workspaces.** Opens a workspace rooted at a specified project directory and resolves all relative paths against that root. No global state is written outside the workspace unless explicitly requested. - **Deterministic command execution.** Runs shell commands with a fixed, documented environment derived from the project configuration and the invoking shell. Environment inheritance is opt-in via flags, not implicit. - **Flag-driven configuration.** Behavior is controlled entirely through command-line flags and an optional project-local configuration file. Flags take precedence over file values; there is no other configuration source. - **Machine-readable output.** Supports structured output modes for scripting and CI use. Human-readable output is the default; structured output is enabled explicitly. - **Exit code discipline.** Distinguishes success, usage errors, configuration errors, and runtime failures via distinct exit codes. No command exits zero on partial failure. - **Dry-run support.** Commands that mutate workspace state accept a dry-run flag that reports intended actions without performing them. Dry-run is not a guarantee of atomicity and does not validate downstream side effects. - **Idempotent setup steps.** Initialization and scaffolding operations are safe to re-run; existing artifacts are detected and skipped rather than overwritten unless a force flag is supplied. - **No network dependency for core operations.** Workspace creation, inspection, and local command execution do not require network access. Any operation that does contact a remote is gated behind an explicit flag and documented as such. - **Scope limitations.** Does not manage dependencies, provision runtimes, or sandbox executed commands. It assumes the host shell and toolchain are already present and does not attempt to repair or isolate them. - **Single-project focus.** Operates on one project root per invocation. Multi-project orchestration is out of scope and is not planned as part of the current interface. ## How It Works The workbench operates in three stages: discovery, planning, and execution. **Discovery** walks the current directory tree, identifies project manifests and lockfiles, and builds an in-memory model of the workspace. It reads manifest metadata such as declared dependencies, package manager hints, and script entries. No files are modified during discovery. Symlinks are followed only when they resolve inside the workspace root; cycles are detected and reported rather than traversed repeatedly. Discovery is bounded by a configurable depth limit and skips paths matched by ignore rules, which include common build and cache directories. **Planning** converts the discovered model into an ordered list of actions. Each action is derived from a manifest fact, not from heuristics about file contents, so the plan is deterministic for a given workspace state. The planner resolves ordering constraints between actions—for example, a manifest-derived step that depends on another manifest being read first—and detects conflicts where two actions target the same output. When conflicts exist, the planner reports them and withholds the affected actions unless a precedence rule is configured. The full plan can be printed without execution. **Execution** applies the planned actions sequentially. Each action is validated immediately before it runs; if the workspace changed since planning, the action is re-checked against the current state and skipped or re-planned if stale. Write actions are performed atomically where the platform permits, using a temporary file followed by a rename. The workbench keeps no persistent daemon and no global state: all state lives in memory for the duration of the process, and any on-disk artifacts are limited to the outputs named in the plan. On failure, execution stops by default and the exit code reflects the failing stage; a continue-on-error mode applies remaining independent actions and aggregates results. Scope is deliberately narrow. The workbench reasons only about manifests and lockfiles it recognizes; unknown formats are surfaced during discovery and left untouched. It does not infer intent from source code, does not resolve dependency graphs itself, and does not guarantee that applying a plan yields a working build—those outcomes depend on the underlying package managers and toolchains invoked. Concurrency is limited to independent read-only stages; write actions are serialized to keep ordering predictable. Behavior is a function of the workspace contents and the supplied flags, and the tool makes no network calls during discovery or planning. ## Modules and Settings ### Project Scaffolding Module This module creates the initial structure for a new workbench project so that configuration, task tracking, and working directories start from a consistent layout. - Project name and scaffolding profile selection determine which configuration files, task records, and working directories are laid out. - An adoption control decides whether an existing directory is incorporated into the workbench or left untouched, so pre-existing content is handled deliberately. - A post-run summary lists the files and folders that were created, giving a visible account of the resulting structure. ### Workspace Registry Module This module maintains the list of projects tracked by the workbench and provides a starting overview for every session. - Add, rename, and remove actions keep the set of tracked projects current, while an active-project control determines which project other modules operate on by default. - Tag and state filters narrow listings so the user sees only the projects relevant to the current context. - The registry view presents registered projects and their status compactly, and serves as the selection source for batch operations and workbench-level status. ### Work Item Tracking Module This module holds the local record of tasks per project and reports every state change in the console. - Titles, descriptions, and priorities can be set and edited, and work items move through defined states until they are closed. - State transitions are reported in the console as they happen, keeping the record of in-progress, blocked, and done work visible without leaving the terminal. - Work items created here form the source for the pending-item listings used in batch operations and the status view. ### Template Generation Module This module produces common project files from parameterized templates and controls exactly what gets written. - Template choice and supplied field values determine which file is generated and how placeholders are substituted. - An overwrite control decides, before execution, whether existing files are replaced or skipped. - The result report shows which files were written or skipped, so each generation step is accounted for. ### Configuration Profiles Module This module keeps settings such as default templates, preferred output locations, and work-item conventions in named profiles. - Profiles can be switched per project or per session, letting different projects follow different conventions within the same workbench. - The effective configuration can be inspected, showing which settings apply and which profile they come from, avoiding silent assumptions. - Settings resolved here feed the scaffolding, generation, and tracking modules, so behavior stays consistent with the active profile. ### Batch and Status Module This module applies operations across several registered projects and summarizes the state of a project or the whole workbench. - A target set is narrowed by filters before the user confirms, and per-project output shows which projects were affected or skipped. - Status scope can be chosen between project level and workbench level, with an adjustable level of detail. - A machine-readable output mode and field selection make results suitable for scripts, while human-readable output remains the default for interactive use. ### Additional Settings - Output format selection switches between human-readable and machine-readable terminal output for all commands. - Field selection controls which values appear in listings and status reports, keeping terminal output focused. - Adoption preference can be pre-set so initialization consistently treats existing directories the same way. - Active project and profile can be set per session, allowing temporary overrides without changing stored project settings. - Detail level for status views can be raised or lowered depending on whether the report precedes or concludes a work session. ## Usage Scenarios ### Bootstrapping a New Project from a Scaffolding Profile **Goal:** Start a new opencode-based project with a consistent structure for configuration, task tracking, and working directories. **Steps:** 1. Run the initialization command with a project name and choose a scaffolding profile that matches the intended kind of work. 2. Set the adoption control so an existing directory is either incorporated into the workbench or left untouched, depending on whether the folder already contains content. 3. Review the post-run summary listing the files and folders that were created. 4. Adjust the active project in the workspace registry so subsequent commands target the new entry, and inspect the effective configuration to confirm which profile is in effect. **Expected result:** A concise terminal summary of the created layout, followed by a registry view showing the new project as active with its tags and state visible. ### Coordinating Work Items and Generated Files Across a Session **Goal:** Keep a local record of tasks current while producing accompanying project files such as notes or changelogs. **Steps:** 1. Create several work items with titles, descriptions, and priorities, then move one into a blocked state and report the transition in the console. 2. Generate a changelog file by choosing the appropriate template and supplying the required field values. 3. Set the overwrite control to skip existing files before executing the generation. 4. Check the result report to see which files were written and which were skipped. 5. List pending work items filtered by state to confirm what remains open. **Expected result:** Console reports of each state change, a generation summary naming the written and skipped files, and a focused pending-item listing for the current project. ### Running a Workbench-Wide Status Check and Batch Refresh **Goal:** Get an overview across several tracked projects and refresh derived files in one pass before ending a work session. **Steps:** 1. Review the registry listing filtered by tag to narrow down the projects relevant to the current context. 2. Run a batch operation to refresh derived files, narrowing the target set with filters and confirming before execution. 3. Inspect the per-project output to see which projects were affected and which were skipped. 4. Request a workbench-level status report with a raised detail level, and switch the output format to machine-readable with selected fields if the result will be fed into another terminal workflow. **Expected result:** Per-project batch results, followed by a single concise report summarizing open work items and effective configuration across the workbench in the chosen output format. ## Usage Invoke the tool by its executable name, `opencode-project-workbench`, followed by a subcommand and any options. Running it with no arguments prints a short synopsis and exits with a non-zero status. ``` opencode-project-workbench [options] [arguments] ``` The tool operates on a single project directory at a time. By default it uses the current working directory; pass `--project ` to target another directory explicitly. Paths are resolved relative to the invoking shell unless `--project` is given, in which case they are resolved relative to that directory. Subcommands are grouped into read-only inspection commands and mutating commands. Inspection commands produce output on stdout and do not modify the project. Mutating commands write to the project and are idempotent where documented in their individual descriptions. Common global options accepted before or after the subcommand: - `--project ` — select the project root. Defaults to the current directory. - `--format ` — output format. Defaults to `text`. `json` is stable and intended for scripting. - `--quiet` — suppress non-error diagnostics on stderr. - `--verbose` — emit additional diagnostics on stderr. Ignored when `--quiet` is set. - `--dry-run` — for mutating commands, report intended changes without applying them. Run `opencode-project-workbench help ` for the options specific to a subcommand. Subcommand help reflects the exact flag set accepted by the installed version. Exit status is zero on success and non-zero on failure; distinct non-zero codes are documented under Exit codes. When `--format json` is used, errors are reported as a single JSON object on stderr. stdout is not written on failure. The tool does not manage dependencies, environments, or toolchain versions beyond what it documents per subcommand. It assumes the project directory is well-formed for the operations requested and reports malformed input rather than attempting repair unless a subcommand explicitly states otherwise. ## Flags The workbench accepts the following flags. Flags may be combined unless noted. Values shown are the default behavior when the flag is omitted. - `--workspace ` — Sets the working directory for the session. Relative paths resolve from the current directory. Defaults to the current directory. If the path does not exist, the tool exits with a non-zero status rather than creating it. - `--config ` — Loads configuration from the given file instead of the default location. The file must already exist and be readable; the tool does not generate it. Errors reading or parsing the file are reported to stderr and terminate the run. - `--profile ` — Selects a named profile from the loaded configuration. If the profile is undefined, the tool exits with a non-zero status and lists the profiles it found. Defaults to the configuration's default profile, if any. - `--format ` — Sets output format. Accepted values are `text` and `json`. Defaults to `text`. In `json` mode, structured records are written to stdout and diagnostics to stderr; the two streams are not interleaved. - `--verbose` — Enables additional diagnostic output on stderr. Does not alter stdout content in `json` mode beyond what the format defines. - `--quiet` — Suppresses non-error output on stderr. Errors are still reported. Combining with `--verbose` is permitted; the last one specified takes precedence. - `--dry-run` — Computes and reports the actions that would be taken without applying them. Output reflects the resolved configuration and workspace state at the time of the run. No files are written. - `--no-color` — Disables ANSI color in terminal output. Color is also suppressed automatically when stdout is not a terminal. - `--timeout ` — Sets an upper bound on long-running operations, as a positive integer. When unspecified, operations use the implementation's internal defaults. Reaching the limit terminates the operation and results in a non-zero exit status. - `--help` — Prints usage information and the flag list to stdout, then exits with status zero. - `--version` — Prints the tool name and version to stdout, then exits with status zero. Scope and behavior notes: - Flags are parsed left to right. Where a flag is specified more than once, the last occurrence wins unless the flag is documented as repeatable; no flags in the current version are repeatable. - Unknown flags are treated as errors: the tool prints a message to stderr and exits non-zero without performing work. - Flags that require a value consume the following argument. Missing values are reported as errors. `--flag=value` syntax is also accepted. - Behavior described here applies to the current version only. Flags not listed are not part of the supported interface, and reliance on undocumented flags is unsupported. ## Exit codes Exit status is an integer in the range 0–255. - 0: success. The requested operation completed without error. - 1: general error. An unclassified failure occurred, such as an internal error or an invalid argument combination not covered by a more specific code. - 2: usage error. The command line was malformed, an unknown flag was supplied, or a required argument was missing. - 3: input error. A referenced file or directory was missing, unreadable, or contained data the tool could not parse. - 4: configuration error. The workbench configuration was absent, malformed, or internally inconsistent. - 5: external command failure. A subprocess invoked by the workbench exited non-zero; the workbench propagates the failure rather than its exit code. - 6: conflict. The requested operation conflicted with existing state, such as an output path that already exists when overwrite was not requested. - 7: interrupted. The process received SIGINT or SIGTERM and terminated before completing the operation. Exit code 1 is used when no more specific code applies; callers should treat non-zero as failure. Codes above 7 are reserved. Signals are reported via exit code 7 only when the process handles them; otherwise the shell's conventional signal-derived status (128 + signal number) applies. ## Recipes ### Run against a single project ```sh opencode-project-workbench run --project ./example ``` Runs all enabled checks for the project at `./example` using the default profile. Output is written to stdout; the exit code reflects the aggregate result. ### Limit execution to a named profile ```sh opencode-project-workbench run --project ./example --profile strict ``` Selects the `strict` profile instead of the default. Only checks declared in that profile are executed. Profiles must exist in the project configuration; unknown profile names fail with a non-zero exit code. ### Fail fast on the first error ```sh opencode-project-workbench run --project ./example --fail-fast ``` Stops execution at the first failing check. Useful for pre-commit hooks and CI gates where the full report is not needed. Without this flag, all checks run and failures are aggregated. ### Emit machine-readable results ```sh opencode-project-workbench run --project ./example --format json ``` Writes a single JSON document to stdout instead of human-readable text. The schema is stable within a major version. Diagnostics and warnings go to stderr so stdout remains parseable. ### Run and capture results for later comparison ```sh opencode-project-workbench run --project ./example --format json > results.json ``` Redirects the JSON report to a file. This is a shell-level example; the tool does not manage report files itself and performs no retention or rotation. ### Check a project without executing checks ```sh opencode-project-workbench check --project ./example ``` Validates project layout and configuration without running checks. Reports missing files, unknown flags, and invalid profile references. Exits non-zero on validation errors. This does not guarantee checks will pass, only that the project is well-formed. ### Inspect resolved configuration ```sh opencode-project-workbench config --project ./example ``` Prints the effective configuration after defaults, profile selection, and flag overrides are applied. Useful for confirming which settings actually take effect. Sensitive values, if any, are redacted. ### List available profiles ```sh opencode-project-workbench profiles --project ./example ``` Prints the names of profiles defined for the project, one per line. Intended for scripting; the output format is plain text and stable within a major version. ### Scope notes These recipes assume the default working directory contains a valid project or that `--project` points to one. Behavior for nested projects, symlinked paths, and concurrent runs is not specified by this section; consult the Flags and Exit codes sections for the contract each invocation upholds.
