--- Sonyvegas is a purpose-built alternative access tool designed to interface directly with the target project's underlying architecture, providing a streamlined pathway for programmatic interaction and control. It implements a focused set of technical primitives that map cleanly onto the host application's core operations, enabling deterministic behavior across supported workflows. The tool is engineered for reliability and predictable execution, with an emphasis on clear internal contracts and minimal overhead. Configuration and runtime parameters are handled through a compact, self-contained interface that keeps integration straightforward for technical users. ## ✅ Requirements - Windows 10 or Windows 11 - PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) - Active network connection - No admin rights needed ## Features - **Deterministic session engine** — Sonyvegas maintains a reproducible internal state model so every operation yields consistent, auditable results across runs. - **Programmatic control surface** — A clean, documented API exposes core functionality for scripting and automation without requiring manual interaction. - **Adapter-based architecture** — Pluggable adapters normalize inputs and outputs, letting Sonyvegas integrate with varied workflows while keeping the core isolated and stable. - **Granular configuration** — Fine-grained options cover timing, concurrency, and output formatting, with sensible defaults for immediate use. - **Structured logging and diagnostics** — Verbose event streams and machine-readable logs make behavior observable and troubleshooting straightforward. - **Resource-aware execution** — Built-in throttling and bounded queues keep memory and CPU usage predictable under load. - **Cross-platform runtime** — Consistent behavior across supported operating systems with no platform-specific dependencies in the core. - **Extensible pipeline hooks** — Pre- and post-processing hooks allow custom logic to be layered in without modifying Sonyvegas internals. - **Lightweight footprint** — Minimal dependency surface and a compact runtime keep startup fast and deployment simple. ## How it works Sonyvegas operates as a thin orchestration layer between your application and the target project's native runtime. It does not reimplement the target's logic; instead, it intercepts calls at the boundary, normalizes arguments and environment state, and forwards them through the project's own execution path. This keeps behavior aligned with upstream releases while giving you a stable, uniform entry point. The core is a request pipeline with three stages: a resolver, an adapter, and a lifecycle manager. The resolver maps your configured profile to the target project's expected entry surface, handling version drift through capability detection rather than hardcoded version checks. The adapter translates incoming calls into the target's native interface, applying defaults and coercion rules before dispatch. The lifecycle manager governs initialization, teardown, and reuse of the underlying runtime so repeated operations avoid redundant setup cost. State is kept explicit and scoped. Configuration is loaded once at startup into an immutable context, and per-call options are merged at runtime without mutating shared state. Sessions, if enabled, are tracked by handle rather than global reference, which makes concurrent use predictable and teardown deterministic. Errors from the target are passed through with their original semantics preserved, wrapped only with enough context to identify the failing stage. For extensibility, Sonyvegas exposes hooks at each pipeline boundary. A pre-dispatch hook can adjust arguments; a post-dispatch hook can observe results; and a resolver hook lets you register additional entry mappings. These hooks run synchronously in a defined order, so composition is predictable. The tool stays out of the target's internals—no monkey-patching, no forked runtime—which keeps it robust across updates and easy to reason about during debugging. ## Modules and Settings ### Project Structure Browser Provides a readable outline of a working project so users can navigate tracks, events and media references without relying on the timeline canvas. - Filter controls narrow the outline by track type or media kind, so only relevant entries remain visible. - Selecting an entry reveals its basic properties in a side detail area for quick inspection. - The outline refreshes as edits are made elsewhere in sonyvegas, keeping the view aligned with the working project. ### Track and Event Editor Offers form-style adjustment of individual tracks and events for users who need a direct way to change settings rather than canvas manipulation. - Mute, solo, level, timing offset and enabled-state fields apply changes to the working project as they are confirmed. - Updated values appear next to each affected entry in the structure browser, giving immediate visible feedback. - The editor targets one track or event at a time, which keeps changes deliberate and easy to trace. ### Render Configuration Panel Exposes output format, resolution, frame rate and destination as selectable fields in a single dedicated panel. - A summary of the chosen combination is displayed for review before it is committed to the project. - Field selections feed the preset system described below, so a familiar render profile can be recalled rather than rebuilt. - Unresolved media references flagged by the auditing module are surfaced here as a reminder before rendering settings are finalized. ### Media Reference Auditor Lists the media files a project depends on and highlights references that cannot be found at their recorded locations. - Each flagged reference carries a status marker showing resolved or unresolved. - Users can review a flagged entry and choose a replacement location, which updates the marker once the reference is satisfied. - Audit results stay visible while other modules are in use, so replacements can be handled between editing steps. ### Preset Manager Captures a set of current project or render settings under a name for later reuse across sessions. - Presets can be reviewed, renamed and applied to the open project from a single list. - Applying a preset produces a before-and-after summary showing exactly which values differ. - Presets draw from render panel selections and track or event states, tying the configuration modules together. ### Batch Review and Operation Log Combines side-by-side comparison of multiple items with a chronological record of actions, giving users oversight of bulk and individual changes. - Multiple tracks, events or render profiles can be selected and compared in one view. - A shared field can be adjusted across the selection, with each affected item listed alongside its prior value in a consolidated change report. - The operation log records what was changed and when, and any logged operation can be reverted to restore the affected settings, with the log kept visible in a side panel for reference. ### Additional Settings - Change highlighting toggles whether prior values remain visible after a batch adjustment or preset application. - Log detail level controls how much context each operation record includes, from setting names alone to fuller descriptions. - Confirmation prompts for preset application and batch edits can be enabled or disabled depending on preferred workflow. - Metadata fields for title, author notes and custom labels are edited in their own panel and stored with the project for display on later opens. ## Usage Scenarios ### Auditing Media References Before a Render Session **Goal:** Confirm that every media file a project depends on is reachable before configuring render settings, so a batch render is not interrupted by missing source files. **Steps:** 1. Open the existing project in sonyvegas and use the Project Structure Browser to review tracks, events and media references as a structured outline. 2. Filter the outline by media kind to focus only on referenced files, then open the Media Reference Auditor to see the full list with status markers. 3. Review each flagged entry marked unresolved and choose a replacement location for it. 4. Confirm that the status marker for each reference updates to resolved. 5. Open the Render Configuration Panel and check that unresolved references are no longer surfaced as a reminder before finalizing settings. **Expected result:** A project where every media reference carries a resolved marker, with the render panel free of unresolved-reference reminders. The user can then proceed to select output format, resolution, frame rate and destination with the summary shown for review before committing. ### Applying a Saved Render Preset to a Reopened Project **Goal:** Reuse a familiar render profile on a project that was recently reopened, instead of rebuilding output settings field by field. **Steps:** 1. Open the project and go to the Preset Manager to review the list of saved presets. 2. Select the preset that matches the intended output and apply it to the open project, with confirmation prompts enabled in Additional Settings. 3. Review the before-and-after summary showing exactly which values differ. 4. Open the Render Configuration Panel to verify the applied format, resolution, frame rate and destination fields. 5. Optionally rename the preset in the Preset Manager if the profile has been repurposed. **Expected result:** The render panel reflects the preset's values, and the user sees a side-by-side summary of changed settings rather than a list of nested dialogs. Change highlighting can remain on so prior values stay visible for reference during the session. ### Cleaning Up Track Settings Across Multiple Events **Goal:** Adjust a shared field across a group of events and retain a traceable record of what changed, so the edits can be reviewed or reverted. **Steps:** 1. Use the Project Structure Browser to locate the affected tracks and events, filtering by track type to narrow the outline. 2. Select multiple events in the Batch Review view and compare them side by side. 3. Adjust the shared field across the selection and review the consolidated change report listing each affected item with its prior value. 4. Open the Operation Log side panel to inspect the recorded entries, with log detail level set to include fuller descriptions. 5. Revert a specific logged operation if a change was applied too broadly. **Expected result:** A consolidated report of changes made across the batch, each item shown with its prior value, plus a chronological log of the operations performed. The user can confirm the intended edits took effect and restore any affected settings to their previous state from the log. ## Compatibility Sonyvegas is designed to operate across the current generation of x86-64 and ARM64 systems running mainstream Linux distributions, including Debian- and RPM-based families, with kernel versions 5.4 and newer. The tool relies only on standard runtime dependencies present in base installations and does not require privileged access, kernel modules, or custom firmware. On the Windows side, Sonyvegas supports Windows 10 (build 19041 or later) and Windows 11 on both x86-64 and ARM64. It operates within user-space and requires no system-level drivers or elevated privileges. macOS support covers versions 12 (Monterey) and later on Intel and Apple Silicon hardware. Sonyvegas is tested against the current and previous major releases of each supported platform and follows a rolling compatibility policy: deprecations are announced one release cycle in advance, and version checks are performed at startup so mismatches surface early with clear diagnostics rather than silent failures. Interoperability is maintained with the project's own configuration format across versions; newer releases read configuration produced by older ones, and forward compatibility is preserved for one minor version. Where platform-specific behavior differs — path handling, process signaling, or file locking — Sonyvegas normalizes these internally so that behavior is consistent regardless of the host system. Unsupported environments are detected explicitly. When a platform or runtime falls outside the supported matrix, Sonyvegas reports the specific unmet requirement instead of proceeding in an untested configuration. ## Configuration Sonyvegas reads its runtime settings from a single configuration file, resolved in this order: the path passed via `--config`, the `SONYVEGAS_CONFIG` environment variable, then the default location under the user configuration directory. Settings use a flat key/value format with sectioned overrides, and any option omitted from the file falls back to its built-in default, so a minimal configuration is valid. The core options cover connection endpoints, request timeouts, retry counts with backoff intervals, and concurrency limits for parallel operations. Numeric values accept plain integers or duration strings where applicable. Boolean flags accept `true`/`false` and `1`/`0`; unrecognized values cause the parser to fail fast at startup rather than silently defaulting. Logging is configured through the `log_level` and `log_target` keys. Supported levels are `error`, `warn`, `info`, and `debug`; the target may be a file path or `stderr`. Verbose output is opt-in and does not affect request behavior. Per-profile overrides let you define named blocks that inherit from the global settings and change only the keys they declare. Profiles are selected at runtime with `--profile`, which makes it straightforward to maintain separate configurations for different environments without duplicating the full option set. Validation runs on load: unknown keys produce warnings, malformed values produce errors, and required fields without defaults must be present. A `--check-config` flag performs validation only and exits with a status code indicating success or failure, which is useful for verifying changes before deployment. ## FAQ **Is Sonyvegas a modification or a standalone tool?** Sonyvegas operates as an independent access layer. It does not patch, alter, or redistribute the target application's binaries. It sits alongside the host and routes requests through its own pipeline. **How does Sonyvegas maintain compatibility across host versions?** The tool targets the host's exposed interfaces rather than internal implementation details. Version detection runs at startup and selects the appropriate adapter. When an interface changes, the adapter layer absorbs the difference without requiring changes to your configuration. **What happens if the host application updates?** Sonyvegas checks interface signatures on each launch. If a signature mismatch is detected, it falls back to the most recent compatible adapter and logs the discrepancy. You can pin a specific adapter in the configuration if you prefer deterministic behavior over automatic selection. **Does Sonyvegas require elevated privileges?** No. The tool runs entirely in user space and binds only to loopback interfaces by default. Any privileged operation is delegated to the host application through its normal channels. **Can multiple instances run concurrently?** Yes. Each instance claims a distinct port and maintains its own session state. Shared configuration is read-only at runtime, so concurrent instances do not contend for locks. Port allocation is configurable if you need to avoid collisions with other local services. **How is configuration validated?** Sonyvegas parses the configuration file against a strict schema at startup. Unknown keys are rejected rather than ignored, and type mismatches produce a diagnostic with the offending line number. Invalid configuration halts startup before any connection is attempted. **What is the performance overhead?** The request path adds a single serialization step and a bounded queue between the host and the access layer. Throughput scales linearly with queue depth up to the configured limit. Latency overhead is measured in single-digit milliseconds under normal load; the tool reports its own timing metrics so you can verify this in your environment. **Does Sonyvegas store or transmit data externally?** All processing is local. The tool writes logs and state to the paths you specify in configuration and makes no outbound connections of its own. Retention and rotation are controlled entirely by your logging configuration. **How do I troubleshoot a failed connection?** Enable verbose logging to capture the handshake sequence between Sonyvegas and the host. The log records interface negotiation, adapter selection, and the exact point of failure. Most connection issues trace to a port conflict or a host version outside the supported adapter range, both of which are identified explicitly in the log output. **Is Sonyvegas affiliated with the host application's vendor?** No. Sonyvegas is an independent project and is not endorsed by or associated with the vendor of the target application.
